choices: git commit -m "work" — commit everything directly
git add <files> to stage, then git commit -m "message" — the staging area is where you craft the commit
git push — pushing stages automatically
Files are committed as soon as they're saved — no command needed
evidence:
$ git status
Changes not staged for commit:
  modified:   app.py
  modified:   notes.txt
scenarios.hint: `git status` distinguishes 'not staged' from 'staged'. What moves a change from one list to the other?
scenarios.prompt: What are the correct next commands?
scenarios.situation: A developer edits two files and wants to commit only the app.py change with a clear message.
scenarios.title: Staging the commit
scenarios.why: Git's staging area (index) is where you assemble the next commit: git add stages specific files (or hunks with -p), git commit snapshots exactly what's staged. This two-step design lets one working tree produce focused commits — commit app.py now, notes.txt later. Skipping the stage (commit -a) is a shortcut, not the model.

choices: Add the patterns to .gitignore (*.log, .env, node_modules/) and untrack anything already committed — gitignore prevents future tracking; it doesn't untrack the past
Delete the files — deletion is the only way
gitignore works retroactively — just create the file
Move the files to another folder — out of sight, out of repo
evidence:
$ git status
modified:   .env          # contains API keys!
modified:   debug.log
scenarios.hint: .gitignore stops future tracking. But .env is already tracked — what removes it from the index while keeping the working file?
scenarios.prompt: How do you fix this properly?
scenarios.situation: Secrets (.env) and logs are being committed; the repo needs them ignored going forward.
scenarios.title: Secrets in the repo
scenarios.why: Two steps: (1) .gitignore with patterns (*.log, .env, node_modules/, plus !exceptions) stops future tracking; (2) git rm --cached .env removes the already-tracked file from the index while keeping the working copy. gitignore alone never untracks. And the committed secrets must be rotated — removing them from history (filter-repo/BFG) is a separate, heavier operation, but rotation is non-negotiable.

choices: git pull — it fetches and merges in one step, which is what you want mid-rebase
git stash push -m "wip", then pull/rebase, then git stash pop — park the dirty work, update, restore
git commit --amend — amend the uncommitted changes into the last commit
Delete the changes — the remote is always right
evidence:
$ git pull --rebase
error: cannot pull with rebase: You have unstaged changes.
error: please commit or stash them.
scenarios.hint: Git refuses to rewrite history under your dirty files. Where can uncommitted work wait safely while the update happens?
scenarios.prompt: What is the clean sequence?
scenarios.situation: A pull --rebase is blocked by uncommitted local changes.
scenarios.title: The blocked rebase
scenarios.why: git stash push shelves the dirty working tree (with a message) into the stash stack, leaving a clean tree for the pull/rebase; git stash pop restores it afterward (list/show to inspect, drop to discard). Committing half-done work just to pull pollutes history; deleting it destroys work. The stash is the clipboard for uncommitted changes.

choices: git log --oneline — the full history is the only view
git diff (unstaged vs staged/working tree), git diff --staged (staged vs HEAD), git diff main...feature — each compares a different pair
git diff only shows committed changes — uncommitted diffs need another tool
git show --stat — that's the diff command
evidence:
$ git diff --staged
# shows exactly what the next commit will contain
scenarios.hint: `git diff` with no args compares working tree to index. What does `--staged` swap in — and what does `git diff A...B` compare?
scenarios.prompt: What does each diff variant compare?
scenarios.situation: A developer wants to review exactly what the next commit will contain.
scenarios.title: Reviewing before committing
scenarios.why: git diff = working tree vs index (unstaged changes); git diff --staged (aka --cached) = index vs HEAD (what the commit will contain); git diff main...feature = feature's unique changes vs merge-base. Reviewing the staged diff before committing catches debug prints and wrong files — the last quality gate before history is written.

choices: git commit --amend to fold the fix into the last commit (only if unpushed), or a new commit — history is append-only by default
Edit the old commit's files directly — commits are mutable
git rebase -i to rewrite any published commit freely — published history is editable
Delete .git and re-init — cleanest
evidence:
$ git log --oneline -3
a1b2c3 Add login
# forgot a file in a1b2c3; not pushed yet
scenarios.hint: The commit isn't shared yet. What command revises the tip commit — and why does 'not pushed yet' matter?
scenarios.prompt: How do you fix the last commit?
scenarios.situation: The most recent (unpushed) commit is missing a file.
scenarios.title: The incomplete commit
scenarios.why: git commit --amend folds staged changes into the tip commit (replacing it with a new hash). Safe only for unpushed commits — amending published history rewrites hashes others may have based work on. For pushed mistakes, the rule is: new commits fix old ones (git revert for undoing). Amend = revise private history; revert = correct public history.

choices: The commits are gone forever — reflog can't help
git reflog to find the tip's hash before the reset, then git reset --hard <hash> (or create a branch there) — the objects still exist until garbage-collected
git pull — the remote restores local commits
Reflog only tracks pushes — local commits are unrecoverable
evidence:
$ git reset --hard HEAD~3  # oops, wrong direction
$ git reflog
abc1234 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
def5678 HEAD@{1}: commit: the important work
scenarios.hint: `reset --hard` moved the branch pointer, but did it delete the commit objects? What log records every pointer movement?
scenarios.prompt: How do you recover the commits?
scenarios.situation: A hard reset in the wrong direction orphaned three commits.
scenarios.title: The reset that went backward
scenarios.why: git reflog records every HEAD movement — the commits still exist as objects; only the branch pointer moved. git reset --hard def5678 (or branch recovery <hash>) restores the pointer. Objects linger until gc prunes them (default 90 days for reflog entries). The lesson: --hard destroys working-tree state but history recovery is routine — reflog is the safety net.

scenarios.title: The secret committed again
scenarios.situation: An API key was committed to a feature branch and pushed. The branch is under review, not yet merged. The key is now in the remote branch history.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response?
evidence:
git log --oneline feature/payments
c4d5e6f Add Stripe integration  <-- contains sk_live_...
github: PR #214 open, 2 reviewers
choices: Revoke/rotate the exposed key immediately, then purge it from the branch history (interactive rebase or filter-repo) and force-push the feature branch.
Delete the file in a new commit on the branch — the key disappears from the PR diff.
Close the PR and open a new one; the old branch history won't matter.
Ask reviewers to ignore the key and merge, then rotate it next sprint.
scenarios.why: A pushed secret must be treated as compromised — rotation is non-negotiable because clones and caches may already hold it. Then rewrite the unmerged branch history to remove it (safe on a personal feature branch with team awareness). A deletion commit leaves the key in history; closing the PR doesn't delete the remote branch.
scenarios.hint: Two problems again: the key is known (past) and the history still shows it (future). Which order do you fix them in?

scenarios.title: The hook that everyone bypasses
scenarios.situation: The team added a pre-commit hook running formatters and secret scanning. Developers bypass it with '--no-verify' when in a hurry, and unformatted code plus one secret already slipped through to main.
scenarios.prompt: What is the durable fix?
evidence:
git log --oneline -5
b2c3d4e Add feature (unformatted, --no-verify)
# .pre-commit-config.yaml exists but is advisory
choices: Enforce the checks server-side: required status checks on the PR (CI runs format check and secret scan) plus branch protection so main cannot be pushed to directly — client hooks stay as convenience only.
Remove the '--no-verify' flag from git so nobody can bypass hooks.
Send a team email asking everyone to please stop using --no-verify.
Make the pre-commit hook slower and more thorough so bypassing feels worse.
scenarios.why: Client-side hooks are unenforceable by design — any developer control can be skipped. The enforcement point is the server: required CI status checks and branch protection make the checks mandatory regardless of local flags. You cannot remove --no-verify from git; policy by email doesn't survive deadline pressure.
scenarios.hint: The hook runs on the developer's machine, which the developer controls. Where is the one place every change must pass through?

scenarios.title: The Commit That Contained Everything
scenarios.situation: A developer's PR contains one commit titled 'fix login' that actually includes the login fix, a formatting overhaul, and a half-finished experiment. Reviewers can't tell which lines are the fix, CI's per-commit checks are meaningless, and reverting the fix later would revert everything.
objectives: Stage hunks selectively with git add -p
evidence: one commit touches 14 files across 3 unrelated concerns.
scenarios.prompt: What Git workflow produces reviewable commits here?
choices: One commit per push — just commit less often.
Stage with `git add -p`, splitting hunks so each commit holds one logical change with its own message.
Squash everything at the end of the PR anyway.
Put each change in a separate branch from the start.
scenarios.hint: A 'fix login' commit also contains a refactor and an experiment — what staging technique separates them?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Patch-mode staging curates the index hunk by hunk, so the 'fix login' commit contains only the fix — reviewable, revertable, bisectable. A doesn't solve mixed changes; C hides the mixture instead of separating it (the squashed commit is still a grab-bag); D is overkill process for what is a 30-second staging discipline.

scenarios.title: The Release That Pointed Nowhere
scenarios.situation: The release pipeline triggers on tag push. The release engineer ran `git tag v2.0.0` locally and `git push` — then waited an hour while nothing happened. When they finally pushed with `--tags`, the pipeline built — from a tag pointing at the wrong commit, because they'd tagged before the final merge.
evidence: trigger: on tag push 'v*'; last successful release used an annotated tag on the merge commit.
scenarios.prompt: What are the two mistakes, and the correct sequence?
choices: Tags don't matter; trigger releases on branch push instead.
Push doesn't send tags by default (push the tag explicitly), and the tag must point at the gated, final commit — tag after merge, push the tag, let the pipeline build it.
Use lightweight tags so they push automatically.
Tag earlier next time to save waiting.
scenarios.hint: A tag never reached the pipeline, then pointed at the wrong commit — what are the two tagging rules?
scenarios.why: B is correct on both counts: `git push` omits tags (explicit `git push origin v2.0.0` needed), and the tag must mark the commit that passed all gates — tagging before the final merge pointed the 'immutable' release marker at the wrong build. A abandons release immutability; C is false (lightweight tags don't push either); D optimizes for speed over correctness.

scenarios.title: The Commits with Someone Else's Email
scenarios.situation: A developer's commits show the author as `root@localhost`. They set `user.email` last month and it worked — then they cloned a fresh repo and the old wrong identity came back. They've been 'fixing' it per-repo for weeks.
evidence: user.email appears only under file:.git/config of the old repo; ~/.gitconfig has no user.email.
scenarios.prompt: What is the actual problem and fix?
choices: Git is broken; reinstall it.
The identity was set with `--local` (this repo only) instead of `--global` — set it globally once, and use `--show-origin` to verify.
Set the email in every new repo as part of onboarding.
Use a different email per repo for security.
scenarios.hint: Identity keeps reverting in fresh clones — which config layer was misused?
scenarios.why: B is correct. `--local` writes to `.git/config`, which doesn't travel to new clones — the developer fixed one repo while the global default stayed wrong. Setting `--global` once fixes all future repos, and `--show-origin` confirms the source. A blames the tool; C institutionalizes the workaround; D invents a policy to justify the bug.

scenarios.title: The Function That Vanished
scenarios.situation: A critical helper function is gone from the codebase. `git blame` on the file shows only recent refactoring commits — the function isn't in any blamed line. The team is scrolling through months of history manually.
evidence: function validate_token absent from HEAD; blame shows only 2026 refactor commits.
scenarios.prompt: What finds it in seconds?
choices: `git log -S 'function_name' --oneline` — pickaxe finds every commit that changed occurrences of the string, including the deletion.
Keep scrolling through history; it's thorough.
`git blame` the whole repo file by file.
Ask in chat if anyone remembers deleting it.
scenarios.hint: A function vanished and blame shows only refactors — which Git search finds the deleting commit?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Pickaxe is built for exactly this: it scans diffs for occurrence-count changes of the string, surfacing the commit that removed the function regardless of later refactors. A is linear toil; C re-runs the tool that already failed (blame can't show what's not there); D is hope-based archaeology.

choices: git merge feature — merges are always the right integration
git switch -c feature from main — branches are cheap pointers; work isolated, merge when done
Copy the project folder — branches are risky
Commit directly to main — branching slows teams down
evidence:
$ git switch -c feature/oauth
Switched to a new branch 'feature/oauth'
scenarios.hint: A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. What's the cost of creating one — and what does isolation buy you?
scenarios.prompt: What is the standard workflow?
scenarios.situation: A developer starts a multi-day feature and asks where the work should live.
scenarios.title: Where does the feature live?
scenarios.why: git switch -c (or checkout -b) creates a branch — a 41-byte pointer, essentially free — so the feature develops in isolation: main stays deployable, the feature's history stays reviewable, and integration happens deliberately via merge/PR. Direct-to-main commits for multi-day work entangle unfinished code with the deployable line.

choices: Resolve the conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>), choosing or combining the changes, then git add the file and commit — the merge commit records the resolution
Delete the file and re-checkout — conflicts mean the merge failed permanently
Pick one side with git checkout --ours for everything — manual resolution is unnecessary
Conflicts resolve themselves on the next pull — wait it out
scenarios.hint: The markers show both versions. Who decides the correct result — and how does Git learn the decision?
scenarios.prompt: How do you resolve it?
scenarios.situation: A merge stops with conflict markers in app.py.
scenarios.title: The conflict markers
scenarios.why: Conflicts are Git asking a human to decide: edit the file to the correct result (either side or a combination), remove the markers, git add to mark resolved, then commit to complete the merge. --ours/--theirs auto-picks are for mechanical cases (and dangerous as a default). The merge commit then permanently records how the conflict was resolved — future archaeology thanks you.

choices: Merge is always better — rebase rewrites history
Rebase for private/local history (linear, reviewable); merge for shared/public history (preserves true chronology) — the rule follows who has seen the commits
Rebase everything including main — linear history is mandatory
Never rebase — it's too dangerous for any use
evidence:
$ git rebase main  # on private feature branch
# clean linear history, then PR
scenarios.hint: Rebase rewrites commits. When is rewriting safe — when you're the only one who's seen them, or after they've been pushed and pulled?
scenarios.prompt: When is each appropriate?
scenarios.situation: A team debates rebase vs merge for feature branches.
scenarios.title: Rebase or merge?
scenarios.why: The policy follows visibility: rebase private branches (yours, unpushed or PR-only) for a clean linear narrative — reviewers see the feature as a logical sequence on current main. Merge shared branches (main, release) to preserve true history — rebasing those rewrites commits others built on. 'Golden rule of rebasing': never rebase commits that exist outside your repository.

choices: git cherry-pick is only for branches — it can't move commits
git cherry-pick <hash> on main — replays that commit's diff onto the current branch
Manually retype the fix on main — cherry-pick doesn't work across branches
Merge the whole feature branch into main — partial merges are impossible
evidence:
$ git switch main
$ git cherry-pick a1b2c3
# fix lands on main without the rest of the feature
scenarios.hint: You need one commit's changes, not its branch. What command replays a single commit elsewhere?
scenarios.prompt: How do you port just the fix?
scenarios.situation: A critical fix sits on a feature branch; main needs only that commit.
scenarios.title: The one commit main needs
scenarios.why: git cherry-pick replays a commit's diff onto the current branch as a new commit — surgical porting without merging the whole branch. Standard for hotfixes (fix lands on main, cherry-picked to release branches). Caveat: the cherry-picked commit is a new object (new hash) — duplicate application later needs care, and overuse signals a branching-strategy problem.

choices: git merge feature --no-ff to force a merge commit — the branch's existence and integration point stay visible
Fast-forward the merge — fewer commits is always cleaner
Delete the branch without merging — the commits are in the reflog
Merge commits are forbidden — rebase the branch into oblivion
evidence:
$ git log --oneline --graph
* 3f2a1b Merge branch 'feature/oauth'
|\
| * 9c8d7e Add OAuth login
|/
* 1a2b3c main before
scenarios.hint: The merge commit groups the feature's commits visually. What does `--no-ff` preserve that a fast-forward would erase?
scenarios.prompt: Why force the merge commit?
scenarios.situation: A team wants feature boundaries visible in history.
scenarios.title: The visible feature
scenarios.why: --no-ff forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible, preserving the feature as a named unit with its integration point — git log --graph shows the branch's lifespan. Fast-forwarding dissolves the feature's commits into main's line, losing the 'this was one feature' structure. Teams that value archaeology (what shipped together, when) prefer explicit merges; trunk-based teams prefer the linear alternative.

choices: git branch -d feature — deletes are always safe
git branch -d feature (safe delete: refuses if unmerged) or -D to force — and git push origin --delete feature for the remote
Branches can't be deleted — they live forever
Delete the .git/refs/heads file manually — the plumbing way
evidence:
$ git branch -d feature/oauth
Deleted branch feature/oauth (was 9c8d7e).
scenarios.hint: The PR merged. What cleans up the local pointer — and what cleans up the remote's copy?
scenarios.prompt: How do you clean up after the merge?
scenarios.situation: A feature branch merged via PR; local and remote branches linger.
scenarios.title: The lingering branch
scenarios.why: git branch -d deletes the local branch (refusing if unmerged — the safety check; -D overrides). The remote branch needs its own deletion: git push origin --delete feature/oauth (or via the PR UI's delete button). Stale branches accumulate into a confusing forest; deleting after merge is hygiene. The commits themselves remain reachable through the merge commit.

scenarios.title: The commit on main by accident
scenarios.situation: You fixed a typo directly on the main branch and pushed. Your team requires all changes via pull request. The commit is already on the remote, and a teammate's PR is now in conflict with your change.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct recovery?
evidence:
git log --oneline -3
9f8e2d1 Fix typo in README   <-- pushed to main
git status
On branch main, up to date with origin/main
choices: Revert the commit on main with 'git revert' (creating a new commit that undoes it), then make the change properly through a pull request.
Rewrite history with 'git reset --hard HEAD~1' and 'git push --force' to erase the commit from main.
Leave it — it's just a typo and rewriting is riskier than the violation.
Create a new branch from main and cherry-pick the typo fix into it.
scenarios.why: 'git revert' safely undoes a pushed commit by adding a new commit, preserving history for everyone who already pulled. Force-pushing main rewrites shared history and can strand teammates' work. The process violation matters because unreviewed main commits are how incidents start.
scenarios.hint: The commit is public — teammates may have already pulled it. Which undo method adds history instead of rewriting it?

scenarios.title: Merge or rebase for the feature branch?
scenarios.situation: Your feature branch is two weeks old and main has moved on. You need to integrate the latest main before opening your PR. Your team values a clean, linear, reviewable history.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best approach?
evidence:
git log --oneline --graph
* 3a1b2c4 (feature) Add reporting endpoint
* 9d8e7f6 (feature) WIP: report filters
* 77aa001 (main) Security patch v2   <-- main moved on
choices: Rebase the feature branch onto main ('git rebase main'), resolving conflicts once, so the PR presents a linear sequence of commits on top of current main.
Merge main into the feature branch repeatedly to keep it in sync.
Open the PR from the stale branch — CI will figure out the conflicts.
Delete the branch and rewrite the feature from scratch on fresh main.
scenarios.why: Rebasing replays your commits onto the tip of main, giving reviewers a linear history and surfacing conflicts before merge. Repeated merge commits from main clutter the feature history with noise. (Never rebase commits already pushed to a shared branch — but a personal feature branch is exactly where rebase belongs.)
scenarios.hint: The goal is a clean sequence of your changes on top of today's main. Which operation moves your commits rather than adding merge bubbles?

scenarios.title: Trunk-based or long-lived branches?
scenarios.situation: Your team of 30 maintains a release train with long-lived release branches, feature branches living for months, and merge hell before every release. Releases slip by weeks. Leadership wants faster, safer delivery.
scenarios.prompt: What branching strategy change best addresses the root cause?
evidence:
git branch -a | wc -l
47
# oldest feature branch: 4 months; release merges take days
choices: Move to trunk-based development: short-lived branches (hours to days) merged to main behind feature flags, with releases cut from main — shrinking batch size eliminates merge hell.
Add more long-lived branches (one per team) so merges are smaller per branch.
Freeze main for a month before each release to stabilize the merge.
Switch to emailing patches so there are no branches at all.
scenarios.why: Merge pain grows with branch lifetime and batch size — integrating small changes continuously keeps conflicts trivial, and feature flags decouple deployment from release. More branches multiply the integration surface; freezes slow delivery without fixing integration risk.
scenarios.hint: The pain comes from integrating months of divergent work at once. What if divergence never got old?

scenarios.title: The Vendor Drop That Must Never Conflict
scenarios.situation: Every quarter, the team merges a vendor's code drop. The drop is always taken verbatim — local changes to those files are forbidden by policy. But the merge always 'conflicts' (whitespace, line endings), and someone hand-resolves it for an hour, occasionally keeping the wrong side.
evidence: last 4 vendor merges each took 45+ min of manual resolution; twice the wrong side was kept.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct merge approach?
choices: `git merge -Xtheirs vendor/drop` — auto-resolve every conflict in favor of the vendor side, since policy says vendor always wins.
Resolve each conflict by hand as today; automation is risky.
Copy the vendor files over by hand and commit.
Rebase the vendor branch onto main.
scenarios.hint: A vendor drop must always be taken verbatim but 'conflicts' every quarter — what merge option encodes the policy?
scenarios.why: A is correct. This is the textbook `-Xtheirs` case: policy declares one side authoritative for these files, so auto-resolving in its favor is correct and eliminates the hour of error-prone hand resolution. B preserves toil and the wrong-side risk; C loses history and authorship; D rewrites the vendor's published history for no benefit.

scenarios.title: The Recurring Merge Conflict
scenarios.situation: The year-long `platform-v2` branch merges main every Friday. Every Friday, the same three files conflict in the same way, and the same engineer spends an hour re-resolving them identically. This has happened 30 times.
evidence: same 3 files, same resolution, ~1h/week for 30 weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What eliminates this toil?
choices: Merge less often so conflicts accumulate less.
Enable `rerere` so Git records the resolution once and replays it on subsequent merges.
Delete the platform-v2 branch and start over.
Have a different engineer resolve it each week for fairness.
scenarios.hint: The same three files conflict identically every Friday — what Git feature remembers resolutions?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Rerere exists precisely for recurring identical conflicts: record once, replay automatically, with Git still pausing for review. A makes each conflict bigger, not rarer; C is enormously expensive theater; D distributes toil instead of eliminating it.

scenarios.title: The Hotfix While the Feature Simmers
scenarios.situation: You're mid-feature with uncommitted changes and a dirty tree when a P1 bug report lands: production needs a hotfix from main in the next hour. Your options look like: stash everything (and hope you pop correctly later), commit half-done work, or clone the repo again (20 minutes on this monorepo).
objectives: Choose worktree vs stash vs clone
evidence: monorepo clone takes ~20 min; developer has 14 uncommitted files on feature branch.
scenarios.prompt: What is the cleanest approach?
choices: `git worktree add ../hotfix main` — a second checkout sharing the repo, leaving the feature tree untouched.
Stash, hotfix, unstash, and hope the stash applies cleanly.
Commit the half-done feature with a WIP message and fix it later.
Clone the repo again in another directory.
scenarios.hint: Dirty tree, P1 hotfix needed from main, 20-minute clone time — what gives an instant second checkout?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The linked worktree gives a full independent checkout at main instantly — no stash dance, no WIP commits polluting history, no 20-minute re-clone. The feature branch's dirty tree sits undisturbed. B risks stash-apply conflicts under time pressure; C litters history; D wastes 20 minutes and disk.

scenarios.title: The PR That Showed 200 Commits
scenarios.situation: A developer's PR displays 200 commits and 214 changed files, but they only wrote 12 commits. Reviewers are overwhelmed, CI runs against a confusing base, and the author insists the branch 'was fine yesterday.'
evidence: 200 commits shown; author wrote 12; branch forked 3 weeks ago, never synced.
scenarios.prompt: What explains this, and what's the fix?
choices: The branch is stale — cut from an old main. Sync main into the branch (merge or rebase); the PR then shows the real 12 commits (three-dot view).
The developer accidentally committed 188 extra times; reset them away.
GitHub is glitching; close and reopen the PR.
Squash all 200 commits into one.
scenarios.hint: A PR shows 200 commits but the author wrote 12 — what happened and how is it fixed?
scenarios.why: B is correct. The 188 extra commits are main's newer work included by the two-dot comparison — the branch forked long ago and never synced. Merging/rebasing main in collapses the PR to the author's real 12 commits. A misdiagnoses staleness as duplication; C blames the tool; D squashes 188 of main's commits into the branch — catastrophic.

choices: git push — the branch tracks origin/main automatically
git push -u origin feature/oauth — sets the upstream so future push/pull know where to go
git push origin main — pushing the branch name doesn't matter
Branches push automatically on commit — no command needed
evidence:
$ git push
fatal: The current branch feature/oauth has no upstream branch.
scenarios.hint: This branch has never been pushed. What tells Git 'this local branch corresponds to that remote branch' — once, so plain `git push` works after?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct push command?
scenarios.situation: Pushing a new branch fails: 'no upstream branch'.
scenarios.title: The branch with no upstream
scenarios.why: git push -u origin feature/oauth publishes the branch and records the upstream mapping (branch.<name>.remote/merge) — after that, bare git push and git pull know their counterpart. The -u is a one-time setup per branch. Pushing to the wrong branch name or assuming auto-tracking are the two classic first-push stumbles.

choices: git pull — it fetches and merges, which is what you want before a rebase
git fetch origin, inspect (git log origin/main), then integrate deliberately (merge or rebase) — fetch updates your remote-tracking branches without touching your work
git clone again — the only way to get fresh remote state
Fetching is automatic — remote-tracking branches are always current
evidence:
$ git fetch origin
$ git log --oneline origin/main -3  # see what changed upstream
scenarios.hint: `git pull` is fetch + merge in one. What does the first half do alone — and why would you want the pause between?
scenarios.prompt: Why fetch before integrating?
scenarios.situation: A developer wants to see upstream changes before deciding how to integrate them.
scenarios.title: Look before you merge
scenarios.why: git fetch updates your remote-tracking branches (origin/main) without touching your working tree or local branches — safe reconnaissance. Then you choose: merge (preserves chronology) or rebase (linear). git pull skips the decision by merging immediately, which surprises people mid-rebase-workflow. Fetch-then-decide is the deliberate collaboration loop.

choices: Push directly to main — PRs are bureaucracy
Fork the repo, branch, push to the fork, open a PR from the fork to upstream — the maintainer reviews and merges; you never need write access
Email the patch — PRs require write access
Forks are read-only copies — you can't PR from them
evidence: # contributor has no write access to upstream/repo
scenarios.hint: No write access to upstream. What gives you a writable copy you own — and how do changes flow back?
scenarios.prompt: How does the contribution flow work?
scenarios.situation: An external contributor needs to propose a change to a repo they can't push to.
scenarios.title: Contributing without write access
scenarios.why: The fork workflow: fork (your own server-side copy) → clone the fork → branch → push to the fork → open a PR from fork-branch to upstream-main. The PR is the review and integration mechanism; write access is never needed. Keeping the fork synced (fetch upstream, rebase) prevents the PR from rotting. This is how open source scales collaboration.

choices: Merge it immediately — green CI means safe
Require PR reviews and passing status checks via branch protection rules on main — no direct pushes, no merging red builds
Branch protection is only for public repos — private repos don't need it
Reviews are optional if the author is senior
evidence:
# repo settings: main branch, 5 developers, no protections
# yesterday: a direct push broke production
scenarios.hint: The breakage came from a direct push to main. What repo setting makes 'review + green CI' a requirement rather than a suggestion?
scenarios.prompt: What prevents the next direct-push breakage?
scenarios.situation: A direct push to main broke production; the team wants it structurally impossible.
scenarios.title: Protecting main
scenarios.why: Branch protection rules on main: require pull request reviews (with approval counts), require status checks to pass (CI), and block direct pushes (include administrators optionally). Process becomes configuration — the breakage class disappears instead of relying on discipline. Dismiss-stale-reviews and CODEOWNERS for critical paths are the next layers.

choices: git pull --rebase on the feature branch, resolve conflicts, force-push the branch, PR updates automatically — the PR tracks the branch, not the commits
Close the PR and open a new one — PRs can't be updated
Merge main into the PR branch weekly — rebasing a PR branch is forbidden
The PR is frozen at creation — new commits need a new PR
evidence: # PR #42 open from feature/oauth; main moved forward 20 commits
scenarios.hint: The PR is bound to the branch. What updates the branch — and what kind of push does a rebased branch need?
scenarios.prompt: How do you bring the PR up to date?
scenarios.situation: An open PR's branch is 20 commits behind main.
scenarios.title: The stale pull request
scenarios.why: The PR follows its branch: rebase the branch onto current main (resolving conflicts once, linearly), then force-push — the PR updates in place with the same discussion and reviews. (Force-push to a PR branch is the sanctioned exception to the no-force rule; prefer --force-with-lease.) Merge-main-into-branch also works but litters the PR with merge commits; the rebase keeps the diff reviewable.

choices: git log shows the remote branches — that's enough
git branch -r (remote-tracking) and git remote -v (URLs) — know what remotes exist and where they point
Remotes are invisible by design — just push and hope
There's only ever one remote — no need to check
evidence:
$ git remote -v
origin  git@github.com:team/repo.git (fetch)
origin  git@github.com:team/repo.git (push)
upstream  git@github.com:original/repo.git (fetch)
scenarios.hint: Two remotes: origin (yours) and upstream (the original). Which commands reveal this map?
scenarios.prompt: How do you inspect the remote setup?
scenarios.situation: A developer is confused about where push and pull actually go.
scenarios.title: Where does push go?
scenarios.why: git remote -v shows the name→URL mapping for fetch and push; git branch -r (or git branch -vv) shows remote-tracking branches and their upstream links. In fork workflows, origin = your fork and upstream = the original — pushing to the wrong one is the classic confusion. The map makes 'where does this go' explicit instead of assumed.

scenarios.title: The Fork That's 47 Commits Behind
scenarios.situation: A contributor's PR shows 50 changed files, but they only edited two. The PR is full of merge conflicts, CI is testing code from three months ago, and the maintainer can't review it. The contributor insists 'it works on my machine.'
evidence: 50 files changed; author touched 2; fork is 47 commits behind upstream/main.
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and what's the fix?
choices: Their fork is 47 commits behind upstream — they must fetch upstream, sync their fork's main, rebase the feature branch onto it, and force-push the cleaned branch.
The maintainer should just merge it and fix conflicts.
Their machine is misconfigured; reinstall the toolchain.
Close the PR and have them email a patch.
scenarios.hint: A PR shows 50 changed files but the author edited two — what caused it and how is it fixed?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The 48 extra files are the fork's drift — the PR diffs against upstream's current main, so every commit the fork missed appears as 'changes.' Syncing the fork and rebasing the feature branch collapses the PR to the two real files. B makes the maintainer do the contributor's hygiene; C misdiagnoses; D abandons the workflow instead of teaching it.

scenarios.title: The Drive-By Merge
scenarios.situation: An engineer pushed directly to main, changing the authentication module — no PR, no review. The change had a subtle timing bug that took down logins for an hour. The team 'has a policy' of PR reviews, but nothing enforces it, and nobody owned the auth code explicitly.
evidence: main has zero branch protection rules; no CODEOWNERS file exists.
scenarios.prompt: What combination prevents recurrence?
choices: Branch protection on main (require PRs + required reviews) plus a CODEOWNERS file assigning `/src/auth/` to the security team.
A stricter policy document about reviews.
Removing the engineer's push access as punishment.
Daily standup reminders to open PRs.
scenarios.hint: A direct-to-main push broke auth with no review — what makes review mechanically required?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Policy without enforcement is a suggestion — branch protection makes PRs and reviews mechanically required, and CODEOWNERS routes auth changes to the team qualified to catch timing bugs. B, C, and D are all social fixes for a structural problem; the next tired engineer bypasses them the same way.

scenarios.title: The Unverified Badge
scenarios.situation: After a phishing incident, the security team notices several recent commits to a sensitive repo show 'Unverified' on GitHub — authored by the CTO's email address, but the CTO was on leave. Anyone can set `user.email` to anything, so the team can't tell if these are legitimate.
objectives: Enforce signed commits on protected branches
evidence: 4 commits authored as cto@example.com, all 'Unverified'; CTO was on PTO.
scenarios.prompt: What control resolves authorship definitively?
choices: Require signed commits via branch protection, with SSH/GPG signing set up for all contributors — only key holders can produce Verified commits.
Ask the CTO if they made those commits.
Delete the unverified commits from history.
Change the CTO's email address.
scenarios.hint: Commits appear from the CTO's email while they're on leave — what proves authorship cryptographically?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Signatures are the only cryptographic proof of authorship — with required signing, an 'Unverified' commit from the CTO's address is definitively not the CTO's, and the impersonation attempt is visible rather than ambiguous. B relies on human memory; C destroys evidence; D doesn't prevent the next impersonation.

scenarios.title: The Thirty-Minute Clone
scenarios.situation: New-hire onboarding: cloning the monorepo takes 30+ minutes and 8 GB. CI jobs spend 4 minutes of every run just cloning. Developers avoid fresh clones, so their stale workspaces accumulate weird state — which causes its own support tickets.
evidence: full clone: 8.2 GB, 31 min; CI clones 40x/day at 4 min each.
scenarios.prompt: What combination fixes both onboarding and CI clone time?
choices: Shallow clones (`--depth 1`) for CI jobs that only build the current state, and partial clone + sparse checkout for developers who need history but work on one service area.
Buy everyone faster laptops.
Split the monorepo into 100 repos immediately.
Mirror the repo to a local server.
scenarios.hint: Thirty-minute clones tax onboarding and every CI run — what clone strategies fix each case?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Shallow clones eliminate CI's 4-minute clone tax (jobs don't need history), while partial clone + sparse checkout gives developers full history with a fraction of the download — both attack the actual cost (bytes transferred). A doesn't change transfer size; C is a multi-quarter migration for a solved problem; D helps latency but not the 8 GB.

choices: Developers run tests when they remember — automation is overhead
A pipeline that triggers on every push/PR: checkout, install, lint, test, build — fast feedback on every change, blocking merge on red
CI runs once a night — per-change runs waste resources
CI is just a build server — tests don't belong in it
evidence:
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  verify:
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci && npm run lint && npm test && npm run build
scenarios.hint: What breaks when verification is manual — and what does the pipeline guarantee about every proposed change?
scenarios.prompt: What does CI buy the team?
scenarios.situation: A team debates CI; tests currently run 'when someone remembers'.
scenarios.title: The pipeline that remembers
scenarios.why: CI makes the verify loop automatic and uniform: every push/PR gets checkout → install → lint → test → build, with merge blocked on red. Manual verification decays under pressure; per-change automation catches breakage at the smallest diff. The workflow file is versioned with the code — the definition of 'done' evolves with the project.

choices: Run everything serially in one job — simplest to reason about
Split into jobs/stages (lint+unit fast, integration slower, build last) with dependencies — fast feedback first, expensive checks later
More jobs are always better — split every test into its own job
Stages are just labels — they don't affect execution
evidence:
jobs:
  quick:   # lint + unit tests (2 min)
  slow:    # integration tests (20 min), needs: quick
  package: # build image, needs: [quick, slow]
scenarios.hint: The 20-minute job shouldn't run if the 2-minute job fails. What structures that dependency — and what does the developer learn in 2 minutes vs 20?
scenarios.prompt: How should the pipeline be staged?
scenarios.situation: A 25-minute pipeline runs everything even when lint fails in minute one.
scenarios.title: The pipeline that wastes twenty minutes
scenarios.why: Stage by cost and dependency: fast checks (lint, unit) gate the slow ones (integration, packaging) via needs/dependsOn. Developers learn about a lint failure in 2 minutes instead of 25, and compute isn't burned on doomed runs. Parallelize within a stage (matrix builds), serialize across stages — feedback speed is a pipeline design goal.

choices: Reinstall dependencies on every run — reproducibility demands it
Cache dependency directories (keyed by the lockfile hash) — cache hits skip minutes of installs; the lockfile hash invalidates on real changes
Caches are dangerous — never use them
Commit node_modules to the repo — the ultimate cache
evidence:
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.npm
    key: npm-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}
scenarios.hint: npm ci takes 4 minutes; the lockfile rarely changes. What makes the 4 minutes disappear on most runs — and what busts it when deps actually change?
scenarios.prompt: How should dependency installs be sped up?
scenarios.situation: CI spends 4 minutes installing unchanged dependencies on every run.
scenarios.title: The four-minute install
scenarios.why: Cache the package directories keyed by the lockfile hash: unchanged deps → cache hit → seconds; changed lockfile → new hash → fresh install. The lockfile is the correct key — it captures the exact resolved tree. Committing node_modules bloats the repo; skipping caches burns minutes per run. Cache invalidation done right: content-addressed by the thing that changed.

choices: Echo the secret in a debug step — logs are internal
Store secrets in the CI secret store and reference as env vars — masked in logs, never in the repo or workflow file
Hardcode the secret in the workflow YAML — private repos are safe
Pass secrets as PR comments — convenient for reviewers
scenarios.hint: The deploy needs the key but the repo is cloned by everyone. Where can the runner read it without it living in git?
scenarios.prompt: How should the deploy key be provided?
scenarios.situation: A deploy job needs a production API key.
scenarios.title: Secrets in the pipeline
scenarios.why: CI secret stores inject values as masked environment variables — never in the repo, never in logs, scoped per environment. Hardcoded secrets leak to every clone and log; echoed secrets leak to log storage. The rule is absolute: secrets enter through the platform's secret mechanism, and PRs from forks don't get secrets at all (that's why deploy jobs gate on trusted branches).

choices: Three separate workflows, one per version — duplication is clarity
A matrix strategy: node-version: [18, 20, 22] — one job definition fans out to all versions automatically
Test only the newest version — old versions don't matter
Matrices are only for operating systems — not language versions
evidence:
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [18, 20, 22]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: "${{ matrix.node-version }}" }
      - run: npm test
scenarios.hint: One job definition, three runtimes. What CI feature fans a job out across a variable list?
scenarios.prompt: How do you test all supported versions?
scenarios.situation: A library supports Node 18, 20, and 22; CI must test all three.
scenarios.title: Testing the matrix
scenarios.why: Matrix strategies multiply a job definition across variable combinations (versions × OS) — three runtimes from one job block, each reported separately. Copy-pasted jobs drift; testing only the newest abandons supported users. Matrices (with fail-fast and include/exclude for odd combos) are how 'works on all supported platforms' becomes a checked fact.

choices: Rebuild the binary in the deploy job — rebuilding is safer than transferring
Upload the built artifact in the build job, download it in the deploy job — artifacts are the handoff between jobs
Jobs share a filesystem — just use a relative path
Artifacts are only for logs — binaries can't be artifacts
evidence:
jobs:
  build:
    steps:
      - run: make build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: app-bin, path: ./dist }
  deploy:
    needs: build
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { name: app-bin }
scenarios.hint: Jobs run on fresh runners — nothing persists between them. What mechanism carries the built output from one job to the next?
scenarios.prompt: How does the binary reach the deploy job?
scenarios.situation: The deploy job needs the binary built in the build job.
scenarios.title: The binary that didn't travel
scenarios.why: Jobs run on isolated runners — the build job's filesystem vanishes with it. Artifacts (upload/download) are the pipeline's handoff mechanism: build once, promote the same binary through test → deploy. Rebuilding per job wastes time and risks divergence (different dependency resolution); the artifact is the unit that flows through the pipeline.

scenarios.title: CI runs on every push, slowly
scenarios.situation: Your GitHub Actions workflow runs the full test suite, lint, and a 20-minute Docker build on every push to every branch. Developers push often, the runner queue backs up, and feedback takes an hour.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best optimization?
choices: Split the workflow: run fast checks (lint, unit tests) on every push, and gate the slow Docker build to pull requests and main-branch pushes, using path filters and concurrency cancellation for superseded runs.
Delete the CI workflow — developers can run tests locally before pushing.
Run everything twice to be sure, but on larger runners.
Trigger the workflow only on a schedule (nightly) so pushes never wait.
scenarios.why: Fast feedback on every push plus expensive work only where it matters (PRs and main) is the standard shape. Path filters skip irrelevant builds, and 'concurrency: cancel-in-progress' stops stale runs from clogging the queue. Removing CI or going nightly destroys the short feedback loop that catches breakage early.
scenarios.hint: Not every push needs the 20-minute build. Which pushes actually need the full verification?

scenarios.title: The Haunted Build Agent
scenarios.situation: Builds fail intermittently — but only on agent `build-03`. The same commit passes on `build-01` and `build-02`. Retries 'fix' it whenever the retry lands elsewhere. The team has started calling build-03 haunted and re-runs failures until they pass.
evidence: 17 of last 20 failures ran on build-03; all passed when retried on other agents.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnosis and the durable fix?
choices: The tests are flaky; quarantine them.
build-03 has persistent contaminated state (leftover files/caches from prior jobs) — wipe workspaces between jobs, or better, move to ephemeral agents.
build-03 has slower hardware; replace it.
The network to build-03 is unreliable.
scenarios.hint: Failures happen only on build-03 and 'pass on retry' elsewhere — what class of problem is this?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Agent-correlated failures are the signature of persistent-state contamination, not flaky tests (which fail randomly across agents). Wiping workspaces treats the symptom; ephemeral agents cure the disease — every job starts from a known-clean state. A misdiagnoses; C and D don't explain agent-correlated, retry-resolving failures.

scenarios.title: The Flaky E2E Suite
scenarios.situation: The E2E suite takes 45 minutes, fails 30% of runs for unrelated reasons (timing, test ordering, shared staging env), and gates every PR. Developers now merge with failing checks 'because it's probably flaky,' and last week a real regression shipped because everyone assumed the red was noise.
objectives: Apply the test pyramid to pipelines
evidence: E2E fails 30% of runs; 3 real regressions merged with red checks last month.
scenarios.prompt: What is the structural fix?
choices: Quarantine flaky tests to a non-blocking job, push coverage down to unit/integration levels, and run E2E on main/nightly instead of every PR.
Add retry logic so the suite passes eventually.
Hire QA engineers to watch the suite.
Delete the E2E suite entirely.
scenarios.hint: A 45-minute flaky E2E suite gates every PR and real regressions ship as 'probably flaky' — what's the fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It attacks all three problems: quarantine restores signal integrity (red means real again), pushing coverage down makes failures fast and localizable, and moving E2E off the per-PR path removes the 45-minute gate. B masks regressions; C scales human toil; D discards the only tests covering full user journeys.

scenarios.title: The Deploy That Needs a Rewind Button
scenarios.situation: The team deploys by stopping all servers, deploying the new version, and starting them — 8 minutes of downtime per deploy, always at 2 AM to 'minimize impact.' Last month's deploy had a bug; the rollback meant another 8-minute outage while they re-deployed the old version. Deploys are now feared and batched monthly.
evidence: 12 deploys last year; 3 caused user-visible downtime; rollback MTTR 11 min.
scenarios.prompt: What deployment strategy breaks this cycle?
choices: Blue-green (or rolling/canary): new version verified alongside the old, traffic shifted gradually, rollback is a router flip — deploys become boring and frequent.
Deploy at noon instead of 2 AM so everyone's awake.
Deploy less often so there are fewer outages.
Add more servers so the restart is faster.
scenarios.hint: Eight minutes of downtime per deploy, rollbacks equally scary, deploys batched monthly — what strategy fixes the structure?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The strategy eliminates both the downtime (traffic shifts only to verified instances) and the scary rollback (flip the router back), which removes the fear that drives monthly batching. B changes the hour, not the 8-minute outage; C reduces frequency but each deploy stays terrifying; D shortens but doesn't eliminate the downtime window or the rollback pain.

choices: Configure every job by clicking in the UI — pipelines as code is overkill
Write a declarative Jenkinsfile in the repo: pipeline { agent any; stages { stage('Build') { steps { sh 'make' } } } } — the pipeline is versioned, reviewable, and reproducible
Jenkinsfiles are only for scripted pipelines — declarative can't be in a repo
Pipelines can't be versioned — the controller's config is the source of truth
scenarios.hint: Where should the pipeline definition live so that changing the build is a code review — not a click-through?
scenarios.prompt: How should the Jenkins pipeline be defined?
scenarios.situation: A Jenkins job is configured by clicks; nobody knows what it does.
scenarios.title: The click-configured job
scenarios.why: A declarative Jenkinsfile in the repo makes the pipeline code: versioned, reviewed, diffable, and reproducible per branch (multibranch pipelines build the Jenkinsfile on each branch). Click-configured jobs are snowflakes — unreviewed, unversioned, and mysterious. Pipeline-as-code is the Jenkins equivalent of CI workflow files.

choices: Run everything on the controller — it's the most powerful node
Use agents (nodes): the controller orchestrates, agents execute — label jobs to agent types (linux-docker, windows-build)
Agents are only for huge enterprises — small teams run on the controller
One agent per developer — agents are personal
scenarios.hint: The controller holds Jenkins' brain (schedules, UI, state). Where should the brawn — the actual builds — run?
scenarios.prompt: How should build execution be distributed?
scenarios.situation: Builds run on the Jenkins controller; it's overloaded and a security risk.
scenarios.title: Builds on the brain
scenarios.why: Agents (nodes) execute builds; the controller orchestrates. Running builds on the controller risks stability (a runaway build kills Jenkins) and security (builds access the controller's filesystem/credentials). Labels route jobs to the right environment (docker builders, Windows nodes). The architecture: dumb-muscle agents, smart-brain controller — never build on the brain.

choices: Put credentials in the Jenkinsfile as plain strings — the repo is private
Use the credentials store with credentials() binding — secrets are masked, scoped, and never in the pipeline code
Credentials in environment blocks are fine unmasked — masking is cosmetic
Pass secrets as build parameters typed by users — convenient
scenarios.hint: The pipeline needs the key but the Jenkinsfile is in git. What mechanism injects it at runtime, masked?
scenarios.prompt: How should the pipeline access secrets?
scenarios.situation: A Jenkins pipeline needs a deploy key; it's currently hardcoded in the Jenkinsfile.
scenarios.title: The key in the Jenkinsfile
scenarios.why: The credentials store + credentials() binding injects secrets as masked env vars at runtime — the Jenkinsfile references only the credential ID. Hardcoded secrets leak to every repo clone and build log. Scoped credentials (folder/job level) further limit blast radius. Same rule as everywhere: secrets enter through the platform mechanism, never through source.

choices: Let the failure notify whoever — no structure needed
Add a post block: post { always { junit '...xml'; archiveArtifacts ... } failure { slackSend ... } } — deterministic cleanup and notification regardless of outcome
Post blocks run before stages — put them at the top
Notifications are the only post action — cleanup doesn't belong there
scenarios.hint: Stages can fail halfway. What guarantees test reports publish and the team gets notified — even on failure?
scenarios.prompt: How should outcomes be handled?
scenarios.situation: Failed builds leave no test reports and notify nobody.
scenarios.title: The silent failure
scenarios.why: The declarative post block runs conditionally on the build result: always (publish test reports, archive artifacts, clean workspace), failure/unstable (notify), success (promote). Without it, a failed build's evidence dies with the workspace and nobody learns. Post is the pipeline's finally clause — deterministic handling of every outcome.

choices: Copy-paste the pipeline into every repo — explicit is better
Extract the common steps into a Jenkins shared library (vars/*.groovy) and call them from each Jenkinsfile — one implementation, many pipelines
Shared libraries are only for scripted pipelines — declarative can't use them
Pipelines can't share code — each team reinvents
scenarios.hint: Ten pipelines, one notification step. What Jenkins mechanism lets every Jenkinsfile call the same versioned Groovy code?
scenarios.prompt: How do you deduplicate pipeline logic?
scenarios.situation: Ten Jenkinsfiles duplicate the same notify/test/publish steps.
scenarios.title: The ten duplicated pipelines
scenarios.why: Shared libraries (a repo with vars/ and src/, loaded via @Library) extract common pipeline code into versioned, tested, reusable steps — each Jenkinsfile calls notifySlack('#team', msg) instead of pasting 20 lines. Copy-paste pipelines drift until 'the standard build' means ten different things. The library is versioned too, so upgrades roll out deliberately.

choices: Create a Jenkins job per branch by hand — explicit and clear
Use a multibranch pipeline: Jenkins discovers branches and PRs, building each one's Jenkinsfile automatically — new branches get CI with zero setup
Multibranch is only for GitHub — other forges need manual jobs
One pipeline for main is enough — branches don't need CI
evidence: # repo with 15 active branches; Jenkins builds only main
scenarios.hint: Branches come and go. What discovers them automatically and builds each branch's own Jenkinsfile?
scenarios.prompt: How should all branches get CI?
scenarios.situation: Only main is built; PR branches have no CI.
scenarios.title: The unbuilt branches
scenarios.why: Multibranch pipelines scan the repo, discover branches and pull requests, and create a job per branch building that branch's Jenkinsfile — new branches get CI automatically, merged branches' jobs clean up. Hand-created per-branch jobs rot (stale branches, missed new ones). For PR workflows, the PR's own Jenkinsfile defines its checks — CI that scales with branching.

scenarios.title: The Pipeline That Ran Everything on Master
scenarios.situation: The Jenkinsfile has no `agent` directive scoping and no `when` conditions. Last week a feature-branch build executed the deploy stage against production 'because the stage just runs.' The team also discovered builds randomly fail when they land on the old Windows executor.
evidence: feature/login-sso build executed production deploy; build had landed on default executor pool.
scenarios.prompt: What two declarations fix this?
choices: `agent { label 'linux' }` to pin the execution environment, and `when { branch 'main' }` on the Deploy stage so only main deploys.
More executors so jobs never queue.
A bigger Jenkins controller.
Run the deploy stage manually via the UI.
scenarios.hint: A feature branch deployed to production because stages 'just run' — which two pipeline declarations prevent it?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The label fixes the environment lottery (builds always land on compatible agents); the `when` condition makes 'only main deploys' a structural guarantee rather than a hope. B and C scale the broken behavior; D replaces automation with a manual gate that someone will forget at 2 AM.

scenarios.title: The Eleventh Copy-Paste
scenarios.situation: There are ten Jenkinsfiles with the same build-test-scan sequence, each slightly diverged — three still use the old scanner, two skip the scan 'temporarily' (since 2024), and updating the Node version means ten edits. The eleventh service is being onboarded by copying the nearest Jenkinsfile.
evidence: 10 Jenkinsfiles, 4 variants of the scan stage, 3 outdated Node versions.
scenarios.prompt: What is the structural fix?
choices: A versioned shared library (`vars/standardBuild.groovy`) consumed by all pipelines via `@Library` — update once, inherit everywhere.
A wiki page documenting the canonical sequence for copy-pasting.
One giant Jenkinsfile that all services share via symlink.
Migrate everything to a different CI tool.
scenarios.hint: Ten diverged copies of the same pipeline sequence, eleventh being copy-pasted — what Jenkins feature fixes this?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The shared library is Jenkins' DRY mechanism: one definition, versioned, consumed by reference — the Node bump and scanner updates happen once. B preserves copy-paste with extra steps; C breaks per-service customization; D changes tools without fixing the duplication pattern.

scenarios.title: The Credential in the Console Log
scenarios.situation: A deploy token was pasted directly into a Jenkinsfile as a string literal. It's now in git history, visible to everyone with repo access, and last week's console log shows it in plaintext because a debug step echoed the environment. The token has production access.
evidence: prod deploy token in Jenkinsfile line 42 and in 6 console logs; token has production scope.
scenarios.prompt: What is the remediation sequence?
choices: Revoke the token immediately, store the new one in Jenkins credentials, reference it by ID via withCredentials, and purge it from git history.
Delete the echo step so it doesn't print anymore.
Change the token next quarter.
Make the repo private so fewer people see the Jenkinsfile.
scenarios.hint: A prod token is hardcoded in a Jenkinsfile and visible in console logs — what is the ordered fix?
scenarios.why: A is correct and ordered: revoke first (the token is live in logs and history right now), then centralize the replacement in the credential store bound by ID, then purge history (hygiene — the revoked token is already dead). B hides the symptom; C schedules urgency; D reduces the audience while the secret stays valid and logged.

choices: 1.2.4 — patch bump for a breaking change
2.0.0 — MAJOR bump: breaking changes reset minor/patch and signal incompatibility
1.3.0 — minor bump covers breaking changes
1.2.3-hotfix — append a suffix, keep the numbers
scenarios.hint: SemVer's three numbers mean breaking.feature.fix. Which number moves when compatibility breaks?
scenarios.prompt: What is the next version number?
scenarios.situation: v1.2.3 removes a deprecated option — a breaking change.
scenarios.title: Numbering the breaking change
scenarios.why: SemVer: MAJOR for incompatible API changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features, PATCH for fixes. A breaking removal mandates 2.0.0 — the number is a compatibility contract that dependency ranges (^1.2.3 means <2.0.0) rely on. Burying a break in a minor/patch silently breaks downstream builds.

choices: Trunk-based: short-lived branches, merge to main daily, release from main with feature flags — continuous delivery needs main always releasable
GitFlow with long-lived develop/release branches — more branches equal more safety
No branches at all — everyone commits to main directly with no review
Release trains require GitFlow — trunk-based can't do scheduled releases
evidence: # team ships to production multiple times a day
scenarios.hint: Multiple deploys a day means main must always be releasable. Which model keeps branches hours-old, not weeks-old?
scenarios.prompt: Which strategy fits, and why?
scenarios.situation: A team deploying multiple times daily debates GitFlow vs trunk-based.
scenarios.title: Choosing the branching model
scenarios.why: Trunk-based (short-lived branches <1 day, merge to main, feature flags for incomplete work) fits continuous delivery: main is always releasable, integration is continuous, merge hell never accumulates. GitFlow's develop/release/hotfix lanes suit scheduled releases with stabilization phases — but its long-lived branches rot under daily deploys. The strategy must match the release cadence.

choices: Commit the fix to main and cherry-pick later — speed matters
Create a hotfix branch from the release tag, fix, tag v2.4.1, merge back to main and the release branch — the fix is isolated, versioned, and propagated
Hotfixes go directly on the tag — tags are mutable
Wait for the next scheduled release — hotfixes are too risky
evidence:
$ git switch -c hotfix/payment-bug v2.4.0
# fix, test, tag v2.4.1
scenarios.hint: Production runs v2.4.0; main has v2.5 work. Where must the fix branch from — and where must it land?
scenarios.prompt: What is the hotfix workflow?
scenarios.situation: A critical payment bug is in production (v2.4.0) while main has moved on.
scenarios.title: The production fire
scenarios.why: Hotfix branches fork from the release tag (the code that's actually live), get the minimal fix, tag the patch release (v2.4.1), and merge back into both main and the release line so the fix isn't lost. Branching from main would drag in unreleased v2.5 work; committing to main alone leaves production unfixed. The workflow isolates the emergency from ongoing development.

choices: Write release notes from memory — changelogs are approximate
Generate from conventional commits (feat:/fix:) — the commit history becomes the changelog source; each entry links to its change
Changelogs are obsolete — git log is the changelog
Only list major versions — details don't matter
evidence:
$ git log --oneline v2.3.0..v2.4.0
feat: add Apple Pay
fix: null cart total
feat!: remove legacyAuth
scenarios.hint: The history already categorizes every change (feat/fix/breaking). What turns that structured history into release notes?
scenarios.prompt: How should the release notes be produced?
scenarios.situation: Release notes are written from memory and miss changes.
scenarios.title: The forgotten changelog
scenarios.why: Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, feat!:/BREAKING CHANGE:) make history machine-readable: changelog generators group features, fixes, and breaking changes automatically, with links to commits/PRs. Memory-written notes omit and misattribute; git log raw is unreadable to users. The discipline pays twice: better history for archaeology, free release notes.

choices: Long-lived feature branches — merge when complete, whenever that is
Feature flags: merge incomplete work to main behind a flag, off by default — main stays releasable, the feature integrates continuously
Don't merge incomplete work — big-bang integration at the end is safer
Flags are only for A/B testing — not for development
evidence: PAYMENTS_V2_ENABLED = False  # merge the new flow disabled
scenarios.hint: The work takes three weeks; main must stay deployable. What lets half-built code live in main without affecting users?
scenarios.prompt: How should the long feature be integrated?
scenarios.situation: A three-week feature must not block daily deploys or rot in a branch.
scenarios.title: The three-week feature
scenarios.why: Feature flags decouple deploy from release: the code merges continuously (no merge hell, always integrated and tested) but stays inert until the flag flips. Long branches accumulate conflicts and untested integration risk; big-bang merges are the riskiest integration pattern. Flags also enable gradual rollouts and instant kill-switches — the same mechanism serves development and operations.

choices: git tag -a v2.4.0 -m "Release 2.4.0" on the release commit and push the tag — tags are the immutable release markers; attach notes/binaries in the forge's Release
Tags are just branch aliases — move them as needed
Lightweight tags on every commit — more markers, better
Releases don't need tags — the version lives in a file
evidence:
$ git tag -a v2.4.0 -m "Release 2.4.0" 9c8d7e
$ git push origin v2.4.0
scenarios.hint: What names the exact commit that shipped — permanently, even as branches move on?
scenarios.prompt: How should the release be marked?
scenarios.situation: v2.4.0 ships; the team needs a permanent, unambiguous marker.
scenarios.title: Marking the release
scenarios.why: Annotated tags (-a, with message and optional GPG signature) are immutable pointers to the release commit — 'what shipped' is answerable forever, and CI can build releases from tags. The forge Release (GitHub/GitLab) attaches notes and binaries to the tag. Lightweight tags lack metadata; moving tags destroys the audit trail. Tag what you ship, ship what you tag.

scenarios.title: The Release Notes Nobody Wrote
scenarios.situation: Release 2.4 shipped Tuesday. The changelog is empty because 'we'll write it after the release,' the version number was picked by gut feel ('2.4 sounds right'), and nobody can reconstruct what changed since 2.3 without reading 80 commit messages. Support is fielding 'is the SSO fix in 2.4?' questions they can't answer.
evidence: last 4 releases: no changelog, versions chosen ad hoc, 11 'is it in there?' support tickets.
scenarios.prompt: What automation fixes this permanently?
choices: Conventional Commits enforced by commitlint, with semantic-release computing versions, changelogs, tags, and GitHub releases from the commit history.
Assign someone to write release notes before each release.
Version by calendar date so the number is always obvious.
Keep a shared doc where developers list their changes.
scenarios.hint: Empty changelogs, gut-feel versions, unanswerable 'is the fix in there?' — what makes releases self-documenting?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It makes the changelog and version a mechanical output of the commit history — every release is documented at merge time, versions follow semver rules, and 'is the fix in 2.4?' is answerable from the changelog. B, C, and D are all human processes that decay under pressure; only A survives the busy release week.

scenarios.title: The Feature That Wasn't Ready
scenarios.situation: The release train shipped Friday with a half-finished reporting feature because 'it was already merged.' The feature is broken for all users, the rollback requires a full redeploy (20 minutes), and the team is debating whether to roll back the entire release — including three good features — or leave the broken one live all weekend.
evidence: broken reporting feature live for all users 48h; rollback would have taken 3 good features with it.
scenarios.prompt: What would have made this a non-event?
choices: Feature flags: the unfinished feature ships dark (flag off); the broken release is a flag flip, not a redeploy-or-suffer choice.
Longer QA cycles before the release train.
Don't merge unfinished features.
Release on Tuesdays instead of Fridays.
scenarios.hint: A half-finished feature shipped to all users because 'it was merged' — what decouples shipping from releasing?
scenarios.why: A is correct. With the feature behind a flag, 'already merged' doesn't mean 'already visible' — the broken code ships dark, and the incident response is flipping the flag off in seconds while the three good features stay live. B and C fight the reality of continuous merging; D reschedules the pain without removing it.

scenarios.title: The Friday 5 PM CVE
scenarios.situation: A critical CVE drops Friday at 5 PM affecting the auth library. The fix is a one-line version bump, but the release train runs monthly and main has three weeks of unreleased features. The team debates: wait for the train (exposed all weekend), or 'just push the fix to prod' (unreviewed, untested, untagged).
evidence: critical auth-library CVE published Fri 17:02; exploit code circulating.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct hotfix workflow?
choices: Branch from the production tag, apply the minimal fix, run expedited review + CI gates, tag a patch release, deploy via pipeline, forward-merge to main.
Push the fix directly to production; process can wait until Monday.
Wait for the monthly release train; the CVE can wait.
Merge main into the hotfix so it's 'up to date,' then deploy.
scenarios.hint: Critical CVE Friday 5 PM, release train is monthly, main has unreleased features — what's the safe fast path?
scenarios.why: A is correct. It gets the fix to production in hours through a reviewed, gated, tagged path — without dragging three weeks of unreleased features along (which D would do) or abandoning process (B). C leaves a critical CVE exposed all weekend. The forward-merge ensures the fix survives the next release.

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Git Devops as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Branching & Merging Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Branching & Merging is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Branching & Merging?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Branching & Merging issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Branching & Merging is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Branching & Merging supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Branching & Merging failure in Git Devops.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Branching & Merging
evidence: All Branching & Merging components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

Restart all components — Git Core issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Git Core is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
