domains.name: Advanced Git Surgery
domains.description: Rebase, cherry-pick, reflog, bisect, and repo composition — surgical Git for real repositories.

scenarios.title: The Force-Pushed Feature Branch
scenarios.situation: Your teammate rebased the shared feature branch to clean up history and force-pushed it. You had the old version checked out, with no local-only commits of your own. Now `git status` says your branch and origin/feature have diverged, and the commit SHAs no longer match.
objectives: Explain why rebasing rewrites commit SHAs
Recover from a force-pushed branch safely
evidence: git status shows 'have diverged' and git log shows duplicate commit messages with different SHAs on each side.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safest way to get your local branch back in sync?
choices: Run `git pull` to merge origin/feature into your local branch.
Run `git fetch origin`, then `git reset --hard origin/feature`.
Run `git push --force` to overwrite the remote with your local copy.
Run `git stash`, then `git pull`, then `git stash pop`.
scenarios.hint: The commits were rewritten, not just moved — think about what that means for your local copies.
scenarios.why: B is correct. The rebase rewrote every commit SHA on the branch, so your local branch points at commits that no longer exist upstream — there is nothing to merge, and merging (A) would resurrect both the old and new copies of every commit as duplicates. Since you have no local-only work to preserve, the clean fix is to move your branch pointer to the new SHAs with `git fetch` + `git reset --hard origin/feature`. C would destroy your teammate's rebased work; D stashes nothing meaningful and still merges divergent histories.

scenarios.title: The Fix That Must Ship Twice
scenarios.situation: A critical auth fix just merged to main, but the customer runs the `release/2.4` LTS branch, which is three months behind main and cannot accept new features. The release manager asks you to get exactly this fix — and nothing else — onto release/2.4 today.
objectives: Port a single commit across branches
evidence: release/2.4 accepts bug fixes only; feature merges are rejected by the release manager.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct approach?
choices: Merge main into release/2.4 so the fix comes along with everything else.
Cherry-pick the fix commit onto release/2.4 with `git cherry-pick -x <sha>`.
Copy the changed lines by hand into the release branch files and commit.
Rebase release/2.4 onto main and force-push it.
scenarios.hint: You need one commit's change on an older branch — which command replays a single commit?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Cherry-pick replays exactly one commit's diff onto the release branch — the fix ships without dragging three months of features along (A would do that, violating the LTS contract). C loses authorship, the commit message, and the `-x` audit trail, and is error-prone. D rewrites the public release branch's history, breaking every customer tracking it. The `-x` trailer documents provenance so future merges can recognize the fix.

scenarios.title: The Reset That Ate Friday's Work
scenarios.situation: A teammate ran `git reset --hard HEAD~5` on the shared workstation's repo, intending to undo one bad commit but wiping five — including Friday's finished feature. The commits were pushed to origin last week, but the local branch now points five commits back and the teammate is panicking.
objectives: Use the reflog to locate orphaned commits
Distinguish pointer moves from object deletion
evidence: git reflog shows 'reset: moving to HEAD~5' with the five commits listed just above it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fastest reliable recovery?
choices: Re-type the five commits from memory and force-push.
Run `git reflog`, find the pre-reset entry, and `git reset --hard` back to it.
Delete the repo and re-clone from origin.
Run `git pull` to restore the missing commits.
scenarios.hint: The commits were never deleted — Git recorded where HEAD used to point. Where?
scenarios.why: B is correct. `reset --hard` only moved the branch pointer — the five commits still exist as unreachable objects, and the reflog records exactly where HEAD was before the reset. Resetting back to that entry restores everything in seconds. A would lose work and introduce errors; C works only because the commits were pushed, but it is slower and destroys local context like stashes; D fails because pull sees the local branch as behind-by-nothing relevant — actually it would try to merge, creating a mess on top of the moved pointer.

scenarios.title: The Regression Nobody Can Place
scenarios.situation: The nightly build started failing sometime in the last two weeks — roughly 200 commits across five contributors. Nobody remembers changing the failing area, the failure is deterministic, and the team is pointing fingers at each other's merges.
objectives: Apply binary search to version history
Automate bisect with git bisect run
evidence: nightly.sh fails deterministically on current HEAD and passed on the release tag from two weeks ago.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most efficient way to identify the breaking commit?
choices: Read through all 200 commit diffs one by one.
Use `git bisect` with the failing check as the test, halving the range each step.
`git blame` the failing lines to find who touched them last.
Revert the last two weeks of work and re-land it in smaller pieces.
scenarios.hint: 200 commits, deterministic failure — which Git tool does logarithmic search through history?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Bisect is a binary search: 200 commits need only about 8 test rounds (log2(200) ≈ 7.6) to isolate the first bad commit, and `git bisect run` automates it completely. A is linear and wastes days; C finds who last touched the lines, which is often an innocent refactor or move rather than the behavioral break; D destroys two weeks of good work to find one bad commit.

scenarios.title: The Empty Directory on Every New Hire's Laptop
scenarios.situation: Every new hire clones the main repo and finds `lib/shared` completely empty. Senior devs know to run an extra command, but nobody documented it, CI handles it via a special flag, and two releases have shipped with a stale pinned SHA because someone updated the library without updating the pointer.
evidence: the pipeline runs 'git submodule update --init --recursive' before every build.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause — and the durable fix?
choices: The library should be copied as plain files; submodules are broken by design.
It is a submodule: document `git clone --recurse-submodules`, and add CI checks that the gitlink is current.
Delete `.gitmodules` and the empty directory will fill itself in.
Switch the library to a package manager and delete the submodule immediately.
scenarios.hint: Empty dir on clone + pinned SHA + special CI flag — which Git feature behaves exactly like this?
scenarios.why: B is correct. The symptoms — empty directory on plain clone, special CI flag, stale pinned SHA — are the textbook submodule lifecycle: the superproject tracks only a gitlink (a SHA pointer), so clones need `--recurse-submodules` and updates need the gitlink recommitted. A misdiagnoses a workflow problem as a tool defect; C just breaks the pointer; D may be a fine long-term migration but it is not the diagnosis, and it discards the pinned-reproducibility the team presumably wanted.

scenarios.title: The Hotfix That Exists Nowhere
scenarios.situation: An engineer checked out the v1.2.0 tag to reproduce a customer bug, fixed it over two hours, committed twice — then ran `git switch main` to 'get back to normal'. Now the fix commits are gone from every branch, and `git log` on main shows nothing.
evidence: git reflog shows two 'commit:' entries above the 'checkout: moving from <sha> to main' line.
scenarios.prompt: How do you recover the two fix commits?
choices: They are gone — the commits were deleted when the branch changed.
Find them in `git reflog` and create a branch at the commit SHA.
Run `git pull` to download them back from the remote.
Check the stash list; the commits were auto-stashed.
scenarios.hint: Commits exist but no branch points at them — which Git safety net records every HEAD move?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Commits made in detached HEAD are real commits — they became unreachable when HEAD moved to main, but the reflog recorded every HEAD movement including the two commits. Branching at the SHA (or resetting to `HEAD@{n}`) makes them reachable again. A is the misconception: Git does not delete commits on checkout. C fails because the commits were never pushed. D is wrong — checkout does not stash anything.

domains.name: GitHub Actions Pipelines
domains.description: Workflows, runners, caching, secrets, and reusable actions — CI/CD the GitHub-native way.

scenarios.title: The Pipeline That Runs on README Edits
scenarios.situation: The team's Actions bill spiked. Investigation shows the full 25-minute test-and-build workflow runs on every push — including typo fixes to README.md and docs/. Developers now avoid pushing docs because 'CI takes forever'.
objectives: Design workflow triggers with on: and filters
Control CI cost with path filters
evidence: 85% of workflow runs in the last month were triggered by docs-only pushes.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best fix?
choices: Move the workflow to run only on a nightly schedule.
Add `paths-ignore: ['**.md', 'docs/**']` to the push trigger so docs-only changes skip the heavy jobs.
Delete the workflow and run tests locally instead.
Buy more concurrent runners to absorb the load.
scenarios.hint: CI burns 25 minutes on README typo fixes — which workflow feature makes triggers selective?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Path filters make the trigger precise: pushes touching only docs skip the expensive jobs while code changes still run them. A loses per-PR signal entirely; C abandons CI's core value (verified, reproducible checks on every change); D spends money to accommodate waste instead of removing it. Note the team should keep a scheduled full run as a backstop in case path filters ever miss something.

scenarios.title: The Windows-Only Failure Nobody Saw
scenarios.situation: The library ships on npm and CI is green — on Ubuntu. A Windows user reports the package crashes on install. The maintainer realizes the workflow's `runs-on` is hardcoded to `ubuntu-latest` and has never tested another platform.
evidence: three Windows-only install failures in the last release, zero CI signal.
scenarios.prompt: What change gives lasting multi-platform confidence?
choices: Add a manual workflow_dispatch job that a maintainer runs on Windows occasionally.
Convert the job to a matrix over `os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]` so every PR tests all platforms.
Ask Windows users to report bugs faster.
Run the tests in Docker on Ubuntu to simulate Windows.
scenarios.hint: A bug ships because CI only ever ran on Ubuntu — which Actions feature tests every platform per PR?
scenarios.why: B is correct. A matrix makes multi-platform testing automatic and per-PR: regressions are caught at the commit that introduces them, on the platform they break. A relies on human diligence and goes stale; C outsources QA to users; D is nonsense — Docker on Ubuntu cannot simulate Windows behavior. The matrix is the standard mechanism for exactly this class of bug.

scenarios.title: The Four-Minute Install, Every Single Run
scenarios.situation: Every CI run spends four minutes on `npm ci` downloading the same 800 MB of dependencies. The workflow has no caching, and developers complain that the pipeline 'wastes twenty minutes' mostly waiting on installs across five parallel jobs.
evidence: the install step averages 3m 52s across the last 50 runs with identical lockfiles.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage fix?
choices: Enable dependency caching keyed on the lockfile so unchanged dependencies skip downloading.
Commit `node_modules` to the repo so it is always present.
Run the five jobs sequentially to share one install.
Switch to a faster package manager without changing anything else.
scenarios.hint: Identical dependencies download for 4 minutes on every run — which mechanism skips redundant work safely?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Caching keyed on the lockfile turns the 4-minute download into a seconds-long restore on every run where dependencies are unchanged — and it automatically invalidates when the lockfile changes. B bloats the repo enormously and breaks across platforms; C makes total time worse (sequential) and doesn't remove the download; D may help marginally but doesn't address re-downloading identical bytes every run.

scenarios.title: The AWS Key in the Repo Secrets
scenarios.situation: The deploy workflow uses an AWS access key stored as a GitHub secret, created two years ago by someone who left. Nobody knows its rotation history, it has full admin permissions, and last week's log shows a step accidentally printed part of the environment.
objectives: Configure OIDC trust between GitHub and AWS
evidence: the key has AdministratorAccess and was created 742 days ago.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best remediation?
choices: Rotate the key immediately and store the new one as a secret.
Replace the static key with OIDC: trust GitHub's issuer in IAM and assume a scoped role per run.
Split the key across two secrets so no single log shows all of it.
Restrict who can view the Actions logs.
scenarios.hint: A two-year-old admin AWS key lives in repo secrets — what replaces static credentials entirely?
scenarios.why: B is correct. OIDC eliminates the static credential entirely — there is nothing to leak, rotate, or over-permission permanently; each run mints short-lived credentials scoped to the role. A improves hygiene but preserves the fundamental risk (a long-lived secret that can leak again). C is security theater; D hides the symptom while the key remains valid for anyone who obtains it.

scenarios.title: The Ten Duplicated Pipelines
scenarios.situation: The org has 12 services, each with a copy-pasted 80-line test-and-lint workflow. Last month the Node version needed bumping in all 12; three were missed and their builds silently used the old version for weeks. The platform team wants one canonical pipeline.
evidence: 12 near-identical workflow files; 3 on outdated Node versions.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right pattern?
choices: A reusable workflow in a shared repo, consumed via `uses: org/ci/.github/workflows/test.yml@v1`.
A script that copies the YAML file into all 12 repos on a schedule.
One giant workflow in each repo with `if:` conditions per service.
Move all CI into Jenkins instead.
scenarios.hint: Twelve repos, one pipeline copied twelve times, version bumps missed — which Actions feature fixes this structurally?
scenarios.why: A is correct. A reusable workflow is the native DRY mechanism: one definition, versioned by tag, consumed by reference — the Node bump happens once in the shared repo. B recreates duplication with extra steps and drift between syncs; C keeps 12 copies of the complexity; D changes tools without addressing the duplication problem at all.

scenarios.title: The 2 AM Workflow Failure
scenarios.situation: The deploy workflow failed at 2 AM. The on-call engineer sees a red X, 3,000 lines of logs, and a failing step that just says 'exit code 1'. They re-ran the entire 40-minute workflow twice 'to see if it passes this time' before paging you.
evidence: two full 40-minute re-runs preceded the page; root cause was a missing env var visible in the step log.
scenarios.prompt: What should the team's debugging playbook say first?
choices: Re-run the full workflow until it passes; flakes are normal at 2 AM.
Read the failed step's logs for the actual error, reproduce the step locally, and re-run only the failed jobs.
SSH into the runner with tmate on every failure for full visibility.
Disable the failing step so deploys are unblocked.
scenarios.hint: A 2 AM failure, 3,000 log lines, 'exit code 1' — what is the disciplined first response?
scenarios.why: B is correct. The playbook is: logs first (the step's output contains the real error — 'exit code 1' is just the summary), reproduce locally in a matching environment, fix, and re-run only failed jobs. A burns 80 minutes and learns nothing; C is heavyweight and risky as a default; D ships an unverified deploy to unblock — trading a blocked pipeline for an untested production change.

domains.name: Container Workflows with Docker
domains.description: Dockerfiles, multi-stage builds, registries, Compose, and image security for DevOps pipelines.

scenarios.title: The Ten-Minute Docker Build
scenarios.situation: The service's Docker build takes ten minutes on every CI run. The Dockerfile starts with `COPY . .`, then runs `npm ci`, then builds. Developers push small fixes all day and each one waits ten minutes for an identical dependency install.
evidence: line 1 is 'COPY . .' and line 2 is 'RUN npm ci'.
scenarios.prompt: What single reordering fixes it?
choices: Move `COPY package*.json ./` and `RUN npm ci` above `COPY . .` so dependency layers cache across source changes.
Combine all RUN instructions into one giant layer.
Switch the base image to `node:20-alpine`.
Add more CPUs to the CI runner.
scenarios.hint: Every source tweak triggers a full 10-minute dependency reinstall — which Dockerfile principle is violated?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Layer caching invalidates everything below the first changed instruction: with `COPY . .` first, any source change busts the cache for the `npm ci` layer beneath it. Copying manifests and installing first means source changes only invalidate the cheap final layers. B doesn't address invalidation order; C shrinks the base but the install still re-runs; D throws hardware at a caching problem.

scenarios.title: The 2 GB Production Image
scenarios.situation: The production image is 2 GB: it contains the full SDK, dev dependencies, test fixtures, and the git history (the build context wasn't filtered). Pulls take minutes, the registry bill is climbing, and the security scan flags 400+ vulnerabilities — mostly in build tools the app never uses at runtime.
evidence: 412 CVEs, 380 in build-time-only packages (compilers, test frameworks).
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct remediation?
choices: Add a `.dockerignore` and switch to a multi-stage build that copies only built artifacts into a slim runtime stage.
Increase registry storage quota and accept the scan noise.
Run the scanner with fewer rules so the report is shorter.
Compress the image with gzip before pushing.
scenarios.hint: A 2 GB image ships build tools with 400+ vulnerabilities the app never uses — what build pattern removes them?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Multi-stage builds structurally exclude the toolchain from the final image (fixing size and most vulnerabilities at the source), and `.dockerignore` keeps secrets and junk out of the build context. B and C accept the problem; D misunderstands — registries already handle layer compression, and it doesn't remove the vulnerable packages.

scenarios.title: The Mystery Rollback
scenarios.situation: Production broke after a deploy. The team 'rolled back' by redeploying `:latest` — but `:latest` had already moved twice since the incident, so nobody knows which build is running now, and the rollback may have deployed an even newer untested build.
evidence: 'deploying org/app:latest' appears 14 times with 4 different resolved digests.
scenarios.prompt: What tagging discipline prevents this entire class of incident?
choices: Tag every build immutably (version + git SHA) and deploy by digest; roll back by redeploying the previous known-good tag.
Stop tagging images and use digests everywhere by hand.
Deploy `:latest` but take a screenshot of the digest each time.
Roll back by rebuilding the old version from source.
scenarios.hint: A rollback redeployed a newer untested build because `:latest` had moved — what scheme makes deploys reproducible?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Immutable tags give every build a permanent name; deploying by tag/digest makes the running version knowable and the rollback a precise redeploy of the last good build. B is impractical without tags as human handles; C is theater; D rebuilds — and a rebuild from old source is not guaranteed byte-identical to what ran before.

scenarios.title: Works on My Machine — Again
scenarios.situation: Three developers, three different local Postgres versions, and the staging database is yet another version. A migration works for two devs and fails for the third; the bug is a version-specific SQL behavior. Onboarding a fourth developer takes a full day of database setup.
evidence: 'install Postgres (any recent version should work)' — step 1 of a 14-step setup.
scenarios.prompt: What fixes this durably?
choices: A `compose.yaml` defining the exact Postgres version, seed data, and ports — one command brings up an identical stack for everyone.
A wiki page documenting the manual database setup steps.
Everyone installs the same version by hand and promises not to upgrade.
Develop against the shared staging database.
scenarios.hint: Three developers, three database versions, version-specific failures — what gives everyone an identical environment?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Compose makes the environment declarative and versioned: the Postgres version is pinned in the file, so every developer — and CI — runs the identical stack. B rots; C relies on human discipline across machines; D creates contention, breaks offline work, and lets one dev's experiment corrupt everyone's data.

scenarios.title: The Critical CVE in Production
scenarios.situation: A critical CVE is announced in a package shipped in the production image. The team cannot answer: which images contain it, when it entered, or whether the running containers are affected. The image was built from a full OS base six months ago and never rescanned.
evidence: no scans exist for any build older than this week; the CVE was published 6 months ago.
scenarios.prompt: What practice would have caught this at introduction time?
choices: Scanning every image build in CI and failing on critical/high, with the base image kept current.
Manually reviewing the Dockerfile once a quarter.
Waiting for the vendor's security bulletin and patching then.
Running the container with read-only filesystem so CVEs can't execute.
scenarios.hint: A critical CVE sat in the image for six months undetected — what CI practice catches it at introduction?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Per-build scanning attributes each new CVE to the commit that introduced it, while it's fresh and the author remembers the context; failing on critical/high makes it blocking, not advisory. B is too slow and misses transitive deps; C is reactive — you're exposed between disclosure and bulletin; D is a good hardening layer but doesn't remove the vulnerable code.

domains.name: DevOps Culture & Practices
domains.description: CALMS, DORA metrics, blameless postmortems, and shift-left — the human side of DevOps.

scenarios.title: The 'DevOps Team' That Ships Quarterly
scenarios.situation: The company created a 'DevOps team' that owns Jenkins. Developers throw code over the wall, wait weeks for deploys, need four manual approvals, and incidents end with a manager asking 'who broke it?' in a meeting. Leadership believes they 'do DevOps' because they bought the tools.
objectives: Apply CALMS as a diagnostic lens
evidence: 4 deploys last quarter; average 5.2 manual approvals per deploy; zero published postmortems.
scenarios.prompt: Using CALMS, what is the core diagnosis?
choices: They need better Jenkins plugins and more automation scripts.
They have tools but are missing Culture (blame, silos), Lean (approval waste), Measurement (no delivery metrics), and Sharing (no postmortems).
They should rename the team to 'Platform Engineering'.
They need to hire more DevOps engineers.
scenarios.hint: A 'DevOps team' owns Jenkins but ships quarterly through blame and approvals — which framework names the real gaps?
scenarios.why: B is correct. CALMS diagnoses this precisely: the tooling exists, but the value framework is absent — blame culture instead of safety, handoffs and approvals instead of lean flow, no measurement of delivery performance, and incidents produce fear instead of shared learning. A prescribes more of what isn't the problem; C and D rename or staff the dysfunction without changing it.

scenarios.title: Fast Deploys, Constant Fires
scenarios.situation: The team deploys 20 times a day (elite frequency!) but 35% of deploys cause incidents and MTTR is 6 hours. Leadership celebrates the deploy count; on-call engineers are burning out. The team argues they can't slow down because 'DORA says frequency is good.'
objectives: Interpret the four DORA metrics together
evidence: 35% of deploys triggered incidents last quarter; MTTR p50 = 6.1h.
scenarios.prompt: What does DORA actually say about this team?
choices: They are elite performers — frequency is the metric that matters most.
They are failing the stability half: 35% change failure rate and 6h MTTR indicate low performance regardless of frequency; speed and stability must move together.
They should deploy even more often to dilute the failure rate.
DORA doesn't apply to teams with on-call rotations.
scenarios.hint: Twenty deploys a day with a 35% failure rate — how does DORA classify this team?
scenarios.why: B is correct. DORA's core finding is that speed and stability move together in high performers — elite teams pair on-demand deploys with low change failure rates and sub-hour recovery. 35% failure rate with 6-hour MTTR is low-performer territory on the stability axis, and celebrating frequency alone is exactly the metric-gaming the research warns against. C would multiply incidents; A and D misread the framework.

scenarios.title: The Postmortem That Named a Person
scenarios.situation: After a 2-hour outage, the team's 'postmortem' document concludes: 'Root cause: Dave deployed without checking the dashboard.' The action item is 'Dave will be more careful.' Since then, engineers have stopped volunteering details in incident reviews, and the same class of outage happened again last month.
evidence: root cause line reads 'Dave deployed without checking'; action item has no system change.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong with this postmortem — and what should it have said?
choices: Nothing — Dave was the root cause and accountability matters.
It blamed a person instead of the system: the real questions are why a deploy could proceed unchecked and why the dashboard wasn't part of the automated pipeline.
Postmortems are a waste of time for human-error incidents.
Dave should have been given a formal warning instead.
scenarios.hint: A postmortem concludes 'Dave will be more careful' — and the outage recurs. What failed?
scenarios.why: B is correct. 'Dave will be more careful' fixes nothing — the system still allows unchecked deploys, so the next tired engineer at 2 AM will do the same thing. A blameless postmortem would ask why the pipeline permitted the deploy without the check, and the action item would automate the check. A, C, and D all preserve the blame framing, which is exactly why engineers stopped reporting honestly and the failure recurred.

scenarios.title: The Security Ticket, Three Sprints Later
scenarios.situation: The security team reviews releases quarterly. Last week they flagged a hardcoded credential and two vulnerable dependencies in code that shipped two months ago — now embedded in three services and a customer integration. Remediation requires coordinated changes across teams and a maintenance window.
objectives: Keep shifted-left gates fast and actionable
evidence: the credential was committed 63 days before the review flagged it.
scenarios.prompt: What shift-left change prevents this class of lateness?
choices: Secret push-protection plus SAST and dependency scanning in the PR pipeline, so issues are caught before merge.
More frequent security review meetings — monthly instead of quarterly.
A bigger security team to review faster.
Banning the libraries that had vulnerabilities.
scenarios.hint: A hardcoded credential shipped two months ago and spread to three services — what catches it at commit time?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Push-protection blocks the credential at commit time (seconds of feedback, trivial fix); PR-time SAST and dependency scans catch the vulnerable libraries before they merge and spread across services. B and C keep the review late — just less late; D is whack-a-mole that doesn't catch the next vulnerable library or the next hardcoded secret.

scenarios.title: The Shadow Jenkins Problem
scenarios.situation: The central platform team requires a ticket for every pipeline change, with a three-week backlog. Three product teams have quietly built their own Jenkins instances — 'shadow IT' — because they can't wait. The platform team sees this as non-compliance; the product teams see it as survival.
evidence: median pipeline-change ticket age: 19 days; 3 unregistered Jenkins controllers discovered on the network.
scenarios.prompt: What is the structural fix?
choices: Ban shadow Jenkins instances and enforce the ticket queue.
Shift the platform to self-service paved roads: templated pipelines teams can provision and modify themselves, with the platform team as enablers.
Hire more platform engineers to clear the ticket backlog.
Let every team run its own infrastructure permanently.
scenarios.hint: A three-week ticket queue spawned three shadow Jenkins instances — what platform model fixes the structure?
scenarios.why: B is correct. The ticket queue is the disease — it recreates the pre-DevOps ops bottleneck, and shadow Jenkins is the rational symptom. Self-service paved roads remove the queue while keeping standards (templates encode the good practices). A punishes the symptom; C scales the bottleneck; D abandons all consistency and multiplies toil.

domains.name: Secret Management
domains.description: The secret lifecycle, Vault, leak scanning, rotation, and identity-based access.

scenarios.title: The Departed Contractor's Access
scenarios.situation: A contractor's engagement ended Friday. Monday morning, someone realizes the contractor had the production database password, three API keys, and the deploy token — all shared via chat messages and a wiki page. Nobody knows the full list of what was shared.
evidence: contractor had db password, 3 API keys, deploy token; all shared in chat threads.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response?
choices: Ask the contractor to confirm they deleted everything.
Immediately rotate every credential the contractor could have seen, and audit access logs for anomalous use.
Change the wiki password so the page is protected.
Wait and see if anything suspicious happens.
scenarios.hint: A contractor leaves with production credentials shared over chat — what is the only safe assumption?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Shared-via-chat credentials must be treated as compromised on departure — you cannot verify deletion of something copy-pasted, so rotation is the only safe assumption, paired with log auditing for the exposure window. A trusts the unenforceable; C protects the wiki while the credentials themselves remain valid everywhere; D is negligence with extra steps.

scenarios.title: The Wiki Password Page
scenarios.situation: Production credentials live on an internal wiki page titled 'IMPORTANT PASSWORDS' — visible to 400 employees, versioned in page history forever, and copy-pasted into chat weekly. Last month's audit flagged it; the team moved the page to a 'restricted' wiki space visible to 150 people and called it fixed.
evidence: the 'IMPORTANT PASSWORDS' page had 1,240 views last quarter.
scenarios.prompt: What is the actual fix?
choices: Move the secrets into Vault with per-service identities, short-lived dynamic credentials, and full audit logging.
Restrict the wiki page to 10 people.
Encrypt the wiki page content with a shared passphrase.
Move the passwords to a shared spreadsheet with access controls.
scenarios.hint: Production passwords live on a wiki page — what replaces static shared secrets structurally?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The wiki — restricted or not — is static, shared, permanent, and unattributable. Vault with dynamic secrets makes each credential short-lived and unique per consumer, identity-based auth removes shared tokens, and the audit log answers 'who accessed what, when.' B, C, and D all preserve static shared secrets; they just change the container.

scenarios.title: The Key in the Git History
scenarios.situation: During a routine scan, an AWS access key is found in a commit from eight months ago. The developer says 'but we deleted that file the next day!' The key has `AdministratorAccess` and CloudTrail shows it was never used — as far as anyone can tell.
evidence: AKIA... with AdministratorAccess in commit from 8 months ago; file deleted the following day.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct remediation?
choices: Revoke the key immediately, then purge it from history with filter-repo and have the team re-clone.
Nothing — it was deleted the next day and never used.
Just purge it from history; revocation can wait for the next maintenance window.
Rotate the key next quarter during the scheduled rotation.
scenarios.hint: An admin AWS key sits in an 8-month-old commit — what is the correct order of operations?
scenarios.why: A is correct. 'Deleted the next day' is meaningless — the key exists in that commit in every clone and fork forever, and 'never used per CloudTrail' only covers the logs you checked (eight months is a long window). Revoke now (kill the live risk), then purge history and re-clone (hygiene). B trusts absence of evidence; C leaves a live admin key valid during cleanup; D schedules urgency for next quarter.

scenarios.title: The Midnight Password Change
scenarios.situation: The DBA changed the production database password at midnight 'for security,' updating the three app servers they knew about. At 6 AM the reporting service — which everyone forgot also used the database — started failing, and the password is now unknown to half the team because it was changed in a hurry and written on a sticky note.
evidence: password changed 00:00; reporting service failed 06:00; password recovered from a sticky note at 09:00.
scenarios.prompt: What process would have prevented this?
choices: Zero-downtime rotation: overlap old and new credentials, migrate consumers with verification, keep a credential registry so no consumer is forgotten.
Never rotate database passwords.
Change passwords only during business hours.
Email the new password to the whole team.
scenarios.hint: A midnight password change took down a forgotten reporting service — which rotation pattern prevents this?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The overlap pattern means the reporting service would have kept working on the old credential during migration; the credential registry means it wouldn't have been forgotten; verification (connection auditing) would have caught the straggler before the old credential died. B abandons rotation; C changes the timing, not the failure mode; D distributes the new secret to everyone including future leavers.

scenarios.title: The .env File with Thirty Secrets
scenarios.situation: The application reads thirty secrets from a `.env` file baked into the deployment artifact. The file is generated by a script that pulls from a shared password manager using one master API token — which is itself stored in another `.env` file. Rotating anything requires editing files on servers by hand.
evidence: strings on the deployment artifact reveals 30 secret values and a password-manager API token.
scenarios.prompt: What is the target architecture?
choices: Keep the .env files but encrypt them with a shared passphrase.
Workload identity: the service authenticates via its platform identity (OIDC/JWT) to Vault or the cloud secret manager, receiving short-lived scoped credentials — no .env, no master token in a file.
Put the .env file in a private repo instead.
Have developers SSH in and type the secrets at deploy time.
scenarios.hint: Thirty secrets in a .env baked into the artifact, fetched with a master token in another .env — what architecture eliminates the files?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Identity-based access collapses the whole tower: no .env artifact, no master token to protect, no hand-editing servers — the workload proves who it is and gets scoped, short-lived credentials automatically. A and C preserve static secrets in files (just better-hidden); D doesn't scale and puts secrets in human hands and shell history.

scenarios.title: How Should I Work Through This Bootcamp?
scenarios.situation: You're starting the Git & DevOps bootcamp and want a study method that actually builds job-ready skill — not just familiarity. You've taken courses before where you watched everything and retained nothing.

For every domain: read the lesson (learn the concept), clear the scenario drills (apply it under no time pressure), complete the labs (do it hands-on), then prove it in the mock (timed, weakest-areas-first). Learners who skip the loop retain facts; learners who run it retain skill.
scenarios.prompt: What approach does this bootcamp recommend?
choices: Watch/read everything first, then try the exercises at the end if there's time.
Follow the study loop per domain: read the lesson, do the try-it hands-on, attempt scenarios before reading explanations, run the labs, and revisit weak areas on spaced intervals.
Skip to the scenarios since those are what interviews test.
Do all the labs first to get the hard parts over with.
scenarios.hint: You want job-ready skill, not familiarity — what study loop does the bootcamp prescribe?
scenarios.why: B is correct. The loop interleaves reading, hands-on practice, and self-testing with spaced repetition — the combination that builds durable skill. A front-loads passive consumption (the 'watched everything, retained nothing' trap); C skips the conceptual foundation scenarios assume; D does labs without the concepts that make them meaningful.

scenarios.title: Theory or Practice — Where Should the Hours Go?
scenarios.situation: You have 10 hours a week for this bootcamp. A friend says to memorize all the Git commands and CI concepts first, then practice 'later if there's time.' Your last interview had a live Git exercise you fumbled despite 'knowing' the commands.
evidence: Work the bootcamp in this order: Foundations -> Core -> Advanced -> Exam Prep. Each section assumes the previous one — jumping ahead is the fastest way to build shallow, fragile knowledge.

scenarios.prompt: What study allocation actually builds interview-ready skill?
choices: All 10 hours on theory and memorization; practice comes naturally on the job.
Roughly 70% hands-on practice (try-its, labs, recovery drills) and 30% theory — with weekly timed drills and an 80% gate before advancing.
All 10 hours building a portfolio project; theory is unnecessary.
Alternate weeks: one week theory, one week practice.
scenarios.hint: You fumbled a live Git exercise despite 'knowing' the commands — what allocation fixes that?

The 70/30 split with hands-on reps, timed drills, and a mastery gate builds the procedural fluency interviews test. A repeats the failure; C skips the mental models that make practice meaningful; D lets skills decay in the off weeks.

scenarios.title: Where Should I Start — and What's the Order?
scenarios.situation: You're tempted to jump straight to GitHub Actions and Docker because that's what the job posting mentions. But the course has 12 domains and you want the order that builds real competence fastest.

scenarios.prompt: What sequence does the course map recommend?
choices: Jump to Actions and Docker; pick up Git basics as needed.
Foundations first (Git Core → Branching → Remotes), then automation (CI → Actions → Containers), then delivery (Release → Advanced Git → Secrets), with culture threading throughout.
Alphabetical by domain name for systematic coverage.

scenarios.hint: The job posting mentions Actions and Docker — but what's the competence-building order?
scenarios.why: B is correct. The layers are prerequisite chains: pipelines are Git-driven automation (Actions assumes Git fluency), and safe delivery assumes reliable automation. A inverts the dependencies and produces fragile knowledge; C is arbitrary; D puts the human layer before the technical foundation it discusses.

scenarios.title: How Do I Handle the Live Git Exercise?
scenarios.situation: Your upcoming interview includes a 20-minute live exercise: clean up a messy branch history and fix a broken pipeline. You know the commands but tend to go quiet and rush when watched.
evidence: Work the bootcamp in this order: Foundations -> Core -> Advanced -> Exam Prep. Each section assumes the previous one — jumping ahead is the fastest way to build shallow, fragile knowledge.

For every domain: read the lesson (learn the concept), clear the scenario drills (apply it under no time pressure), complete the labs (do it hands-on), then prove it in the mock (timed, weakest-areas-first). Learners who skip the loop retain facts; learners who run it retain skill.
scenarios.prompt: What approach turns the exercise into evidence of senior judgment?
choices: Work as fast as possible to show efficiency; explain at the end if there's time.
Narrate decisions as you type (branch checks before rebasing, verification after destructive ops), follow constraint→mechanism→action→verify, and verify each step before moving on.
Ask the interviewer to look away so you can concentrate.
Memorize a script of commands and execute it verbatim.

scenarios.why: B is correct. scenarios.title: What Exactly Am I Building for the Capstone?
scenarios.situation: You want the capstone to impress hiring managers, but you're unsure what 'a DevOps pipeline project' should concretely contain versus what's just resume padding.
objectives: Scope the capstone as a complete system
evidence: Deliverable bar: Scope the capstone as a complete system; Document architecture decisions. A reviewer with no prior context should be able to reproduce your result from your writeup and repo alone.

Working demo (not screenshots of a plan), an architecture diagram showing how the pieces connect, a README with setup steps, and a 2-minute narrated walkthrough. If any one of these is missing, the project isn't done.
scenarios.prompt: What scope makes the capstone credible?
choices: A repo with protected branches, CODEOWNERS, a full Actions pipeline (lint→test→scan→push), multi-stage images with immutable tags, OIDC-based secrets, semantic releases, and documented process — the complete delivery system.
A Dockerfile and a shell script that deploys.
A 50-page design doc with no working code.
Five different CI tools configured for the same app.
scenarios.hint: What scope makes a pipeline capstone credible to hiring managers?
scenarios.why: A is correct. Credibility comes from the integrated system: each piece (branching, CI, images, secrets, releases) is standard individually, but wiring them together with documentation is what working DevOps engineers actually do. B is a fragment; C is unproven; D is tool tourism.

scenarios.title: In What Order Do I Build the Capstone?
scenarios.situation: You've got the architecture. Now you need a build sequence that doesn't leave you debugging four layers at once the night before the demo.
evidence: Deliverable bar: Phase construction with verification gates; Test failure paths deliberately. A reviewer with no prior context should be able to reproduce your result from your writeup and repo alone.

Working demo (not screenshots of a plan), an architecture diagram showing how the pieces connect, a README with setup steps, and a 2-minute narrated walkthrough. If any one of these is missing, the project isn't done.
scenarios.prompt: What phased approach keeps the build debuggable?
choices: Build everything, then test at the end — integration testing catches it all.
Phase it: repo protections → CI → containers/security → delivery, verifying each phase's checklist (including deliberate failure tests) before proceeding.
Start with the production deploy and work backward.
Build whatever's most interesting first.
scenarios.hint: How do you sequence the capstone build to stay debuggable?
scenarios.why: B is correct. Phased construction with per-phase verification (especially deliberate failure tests) localizes every bug to the layer you just built. A defers all debugging to the worst moment; C builds the roof before the foundation; D optimizes for fun over a working demo.

scenarios.title: How Do I Present the Capstone So It Gets Me Hired?
scenarios.situation: The pipeline works. Now you need the demo and portfolio packaging that converts 'I built a thing' into interview callbacks.
evidence: Deliverable bar: Demo live including failure paths; Quantify results in portfolio artifacts. A reviewer with no prior context should be able to reproduce your result from your writeup and repo alone.

Working demo (not screenshots of a plan), an architecture diagram showing how the pieces connect, a README with setup steps, and a 2-minute narrated walkthrough. If any one of these is missing, the project isn't done.
scenarios.prompt: What presentation approach maximizes hiring signal?
choices: A 10-minute live narrated demo (feature → PR → pipeline → release → flag rollout → failure gates), plus a README with architecture, quantified results, a demo video, and a one-page case study.
A long README describing what the pipeline does.
Screenshots of green builds.
Just link the repo and let it speak for itself.
scenarios.hint: The pipeline works — how do you package it for maximum hiring signal?
scenarios.why: A is correct. The live demo (including failure handling) proves it works and proves judgment; the quantified README and case study give hiring managers scannable evidence; the video survives beyond the call. B describes without proving; C shows green without context; D assumes reviewers will excavate your repo — they won't.

lessons.title: Git Core — Core concepts
concepts: Staging area: git's staging area (index) is where you assemble the next commit: git add stages specific files (or hunks with -p), git commit snapshots exactly what's staged.

.gitignore: two steps: (1) .gitignore with patterns (*.log, .env, node_modules/, plus !exceptions) stops future tracking; (2) git rm --cached .env removes the already-tracked file from the index while keeping the working copy. gitignore alone never untracks.

stash: git stash push shelves the dirty working tree (with a message) into the stash stack, leaving a clean tree for the pull/rebase; git stash pop restores it afterward (list/show to inspect, drop to discard).

Working tree: git diff = working tree vs index (unstaged changes); git diff --staged (aka --cached) = index vs HEAD (what the commit will contain); git diff main...feature = feature's unique changes vs merge-base.

example.code:
$ git diff --staged
# shows exactly what the next commit will contain
example.walkthrough: git diff = working tree vs index (unstaged changes); git diff --staged (aka --cached) = index vs HEAD (what the commit will contain); git diff main...feature = feature's unique changes vs merge-base. Reviewing the staged diff before committing catches debug prints and wrong files — the last quality gate before history is written.

Common trap: git diff only shows committed changes.
Common trap: git rebase -i to rewrite any published commit freely.

lessons.title: Branching & Merging — Core concepts
concepts: Branches: merge shared branches (main, release) to preserve true history — rebasing those rewrites commits others built on. Stale branches accumulate into a confusing forest; deleting after merge is hygiene.

Isolation: git switch -c (or checkout -b) creates a branch — a 41-byte pointer, essentially free — so the feature develops in isolation: main stays deployable, the feature's history stays reviewable, and integration happens deliberately via merge/PR.

Merge conflicts: --no-ff forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible, preserving the feature as a named unit with its integration point — git log --graph shows the branch's lifespan. The commits themselves remain reachable through the merge commit.
rebase: the policy follows visibility: rebase private branches (yours, unpushed or PR-only) for a clean linear narrative — reviewers see the feature as a logical sequence on current main.

example.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
port = 8080
=======
port = 9090
>>>>>>> feature/ports
example.walkthrough: Conflicts are Git asking a human to decide: edit the file to the correct result (either side or a combination), remove the markers, git add to mark resolved, then commit to complete the merge. --ours/--theirs auto-picks are for mechanical cases (and dangerous as a default). The merge commit then permanently records how the conflict was resolved — future archaeology thanks you.

pitfalls: Common trap: rebase for private/local history (linear, reviewable); merge for shared/public history (preserves true chronology).
Common trap: merge the whole feature branch into main.
Common trap: conflicts resolve themselves on the next pull.
Common trap: pick one side with git checkout --ours for everything.

lessons.title: Remotes & Collaboration — Core concepts
concepts: Upstream tracking: git remote -v shows the name→URL mapping for fetch and push; git branch -r (or git branch -vv) shows remote-tracking branches and their upstream links.

push: the fork workflow: fork (your own server-side copy) → clone the fork → branch → push to the fork → open a PR from fork-branch to upstream-main. Branch protection rules on main: require pull request reviews (with approval counts), require status checks to pass (CI), and block direct pushes (include administrators optionally).

fetch: keeping the fork synced (fetch upstream, rebase) prevents the PR from rotting. git fetch updates your remote-tracking branches (origin/main) without touching your working tree or local branches — safe reconnaissance.
Fork workflow: in fork workflows, origin = your fork and upstream = the original — pushing to the wrong one is the classic confusion.
Pull requests: then you choose: merge (preserves chronology) or rebase (linear). git pull skips the decision by merging immediately, which surprises people mid-rebase-workflow.

example.code:
$ git push
fatal: The current branch feature/oauth has no upstream branch.
example.walkthrough: git push -u origin feature/oauth publishes the branch and records the upstream mapping (branch.<name>.remote/merge) — after that, bare git push and git pull know their counterpart. The -u is a one-time setup per branch. Pushing to the wrong branch name or assuming auto-tracking are the two classic first-push stumbles.

pitfalls: Common trap: fork the repo, branch, push to the fork, open a PR from the fork to upstream.
Common trap: branch protection is only for public repos.
Common trap: git fetch origin, inspect (git log origin/main), then integrate deliberately (merge or rebase).
Common trap: git log shows the remote branches.

lessons.title: CI Concepts — Core concepts

Principle: CI makes the verify loop automatic and uniform: every push/PR gets checkout → install → lint → test → build, with merge blocked on red.
Principle: manual verification decays under pressure; per-change automation catches breakage at the smallest diff.

example.walkthrough: CI secret stores inject values as masked environment variables — never in the repo, never in logs, scoped per environment. Hardcoded secrets leak to every clone and log; echoed secrets leak to log storage. Rule: absolute: secrets enter through the platform's secret mechanism, and PRs from forks don't get secrets at all (that's why deploy jobs gate on trusted branches).

lessons.title: Release Flow — Core concepts
concepts: Trunk-based (short-lived branches <1 day, merge to main, feature flags for incomplete work) fits continuous delivery: main is always releasable, integration is continuous, merge hell never accumulates.

Breaking changes: conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, feat!:/BREAKING CHANGE:) make history machine-readable: changelog generators group features, fixes, and breaking changes automatically, with links to commits/PRs.
Branching from main would drag in unreleased v2.5 work; committing to main alone leaves production unfixed.

Release branches: hotfix branches fork from the release tag (the code that's actually live), get the minimal fix, tag the patch release (v2.4.1), and merge back into both main and the release line so the fix isn't lost.

example.code: PAYMENTS_V2_ENABLED = False  # merge the new flow disabled
example.walkthrough: Feature flags decouple deploy from release: the code merges continuously (no merge hell, always integrated and tested) but stays inert until the flag flips. Long branches accumulate conflicts and untested integration risk; big-bang merges are the riskiest integration pattern. Flags also enable gradual rollouts and instant kill-switches — the same mechanism serves development and operations.

pitfalls: Common trap: generate from conventional commits (feat:/fix:).
Common trap: everyone commits to main directly with no review.
Common trap: gitFlow with long-lived develop/release branches.
Common trap: wait for the next scheduled release.

lessons.title: Interactive Rebase: Rewriting History Safely
concepts: Rebase replays commits: while `git merge` preserves history by adding a merge commit that joins two lines of development, `git rebase` lifts your branch's commits off their old base and replays them one by one onto a new base, producing a linear history. The tradeoff is that every replayed commit gets a new SHA — the content is identical, but the commit identity is new, which is why rebasing shared work is dangerous.

`git rebase -i` opens a todo list where each line is a commit prefixed by a command. `pick` keeps the commit as-is, `reword` lets you edit its message, `squash` and `fixup` fold a commit into the one above it (squash combines both messages for editing, fixup silently discards the folded commit's message), and `drop` removes the commit entirely. Reordering the lines reorders history itself.

The golden rule: never rebase commits that exist outside your own machine — never rebase public or shared branches. Rebasing rewrites SHAs, so any collaborator who based work on the old SHAs now holds a divergent history Git cannot auto-resolve. Recovery means every collaborator re-clones or carefully resets, which is why teams restrict rebasing to private feature branches.

Recovery flow during a rebase: when a conflict stops the rebase, resolve the marked files, `git add` them, then `git rebase --continue` to resume replaying. `git rebase --skip` drops the conflicting commit and moves on, and `git rebase --abort` restores the branch to exactly where it was before the rebase started. If you panic mid-rebase, `--abort` is always the safe exit.

example.code:
$ git log --oneline main..feature
a1b2c3d Add login form
e4f5a6b Fix typo in README
c7d8e9f WIP: debugging

$ git checkout feature
$ git rebase -i main
# --- todo list opens in your editor ---
pick c7d8e9f WIP: debugging
pick e4f5a6b Fix typo in README
pick a1b2c3d Add login form
# --- you edit it to this ---
reword c7d8e9f Add request logging to auth handler
fixup e4f5a6b
pick a1b2c3d Add login form

$ git log --oneline main..feature
9f8e7d6 Add login form
3c2b1a0 Add request logging to auth handler
example.walkthrough: The session starts by listing the three messy commits on the feature branch. `git rebase -i main` opens the todo list with one line per commit, oldest first. Editing `pick` to `reword` on the WIP commit lets us write a proper message; `fixup` folds the typo fix into the commit above so it vanishes as a separate change. After saving, Git replays the commits onto main and the final log shows two clean commits with brand-new SHAs — history rewritten, ready for review.

pitfalls: Rebasing the wrong branch: running `git rebase -i main` while checked out on main replays main's own commits — always `git checkout feature` first, or pass the branch explicitly.

Squashing away granular history reviewers need: folding 12 commits into 1 hides the logical steps a reviewer must verify. Squash related fixups, but keep logically separate changes as separate commits.

Force-pushing without `--force-with-lease`: a plain `--force` can silently overwrite a teammate's push that landed after your fetch. `--force-with-lease` refuses unless the remote still matches what you last saw.
lessons.try_it: Create a scratch repo, make four messy commits (typos, WIP messages) on a branch, then run `git rebase -i HEAD~4` and reshape them into two clean commits with professional messages.

lessons.title: Cherry-Pick: Surgical Commit Porting
concepts: `git cherry-pick <sha>` takes the diff of one existing commit and replays it onto your current HEAD as a brand-new commit. Unlike merging a whole branch, cherry-picking ports a single change — the original commit stays where it was, and the new commit gets a fresh SHA, author date of now, but keeps the original author and message.

The classic use case is the hotfix: a bug fix lands on main but also needs to ship on the `release/2.4` maintenance branch, which cannot take all of main's new features. Cherry-picking the fix commit onto the release branch ports exactly that change. Cherry-picking ranges (`git cherry-pick A..B`) ports a series of commits.

Cherry-picks can conflict when the target branch's code has drifted from the source. Git stops and lets you resolve exactly like a merge conflict, then `git cherry-pick --continue`; `--abort` backs out cleanly. The `-x` flag appends '(cherry picked from commit ...)' to the message, creating an audit trail back to the original.

Overuse is a smell: if you find yourself cherry-picking the same commits repeatedly between long-lived branches, the branching model is wrong — consider merging or rebasing the branch instead. Each cherry-pick also creates a duplicate commit that future merges may conflict with, because Git sees two different SHAs with similar content.

example.code:
$ git checkout release/2.4
$ git cherry-pick -x 9f8e7d6
Auto-merging src/auth.py
[release/2.4 4d5c6b7] Fix timing attack in login comparison
 Date: Tue Oct 6 14:22:10 2026 -0400
 1 file changed, 8 insertions(+), 3 deletions(-)

$ git log --oneline -1 --format='%H %s%n(b) %b' HEAD
4d5c6b7 Fix timing attack in login comparison
(b) (cherry picked from commit 9f8e7d6a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d)
example.walkthrough: We check out the maintenance branch and cherry-pick the security fix from main with `-x`, which records the source SHA in the message body. The output confirms the change applied cleanly to src/auth.py as a new commit on release/2.4. The final log shows the `(cherry picked from commit ...)` trailer — future maintainers can trace this fix back to its origin on main.

pitfalls: Cherry-picking merge commits without `-m`: Git needs `-m 1` to know which parent's diff to replay; without it the command refuses or picks wrong.
Porting without the `-x` trailer on fixes that need traceability: months later nobody can tell where the fix came from or whether the release branch already has it.
Cherry-pick chains between long-lived branches instead of merging: every port doubles future conflict surface because Git treats the copies as unrelated commits.
lessons.try_it: In a scratch repo, make a fix on main, create a release branch from an older commit, and cherry-pick the fix onto it with `-x`. Then run `git log` on both branches and compare the SHAs.

lessons.title: Reflog & Recovery: Rescuing Lost Commits
concepts: The reflog is Git's flight recorder: every time a branch pointer moves — commit, rebase, reset, merge, checkout — Git appends an entry to `.git/logs/`, recording the old and new SHA. `git reflog` shows this local history, including commits that are no longer reachable from any branch, which is exactly what you need after a bad reset.

`git reset --hard` only moves the branch pointer; it does not immediately delete commit objects. The 'lost' commits still exist in the object database until garbage collection prunes them (default: unreachable objects expire after 30–90 days). That window is your rescue opportunity: find the SHA in the reflog, then `git reset --hard <sha>` or create a branch at it.

Recovery recipe: run `git reflog`, identify the entry from before the mistake (e.g. `HEAD@{3}`), verify with `git show HEAD@{3}`, then point the branch back with `git reset --hard HEAD@{3}` or `git branch rescue HEAD@{3}`. The `HEAD@{n}` syntax addresses reflog entries directly without copying SHAs.

The reflog is local-only — it is never pushed, fetched, or cloned. You cannot recover someone else's lost commits from your reflog, and a fresh clone has an empty reflog. It also cannot resurrect uncommitted work: only commits (and stashed entries, which the stash reflog tracks) are recorded.

example.code:
$ git reset --hard HEAD~3   # oops — wrong direction!
HEAD is now at b7a9c1d Old base

$ git reflog
b7a9c1d HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
f3e2d1c HEAD@{1}: commit: Add payment webhook
a8b7c6d HEAD@{2}: commit: Fix rounding bug

$ git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
HEAD is now at f3e2d1c Add payment webhook
$ git log --oneline -2
f3e2d1c Add payment webhook
a8b7c6d Fix rounding bug
example.walkthrough: The accidental `reset --hard HEAD~3` moved the branch pointer backward, orphaning two commits. The reflog shows the reset as HEAD@{0} and the two orphaned commits as HEAD@{1} and HEAD@{2}. Resetting hard to HEAD@{1} moves the pointer back onto the payment-webhook commit, and the log confirms both commits are reachable again — nothing was ever truly deleted.

pitfalls: Running `git gc --prune=now` after a mistake: aggressive pruning deletes the unreachable objects your recovery depends on. Never prune when you are trying to recover.
Assuming reflog survives a re-clone: it does not — cloning gives you a fresh, empty reflog, so recovery must happen in the repo where the mistake occurred.
Confusing reflog entries across operations: `HEAD@{1}` means 'where HEAD was one move ago', which shifts as you run more commands — always `git show` the entry before resetting to it.
lessons.try_it: In a scratch repo, commit twice, then `git reset --hard HEAD~2`. Use `git reflog` to find the lost commits and restore them without re-typing anything.

lessons.title: Bisect: Hunting the Breaking Commit
concepts: `git bisect` automates a binary search through history: you mark one known-good commit and one known-bad commit, and Git checks out the midpoint commit for you to test. Each time you report good or bad, it halves the remaining range, finding the culprit in roughly log2(n) steps — 10 tests cover 1,000 commits.

The workflow: `git bisect start`, then `git bisect bad` (defaults to HEAD) and `git bisect good <sha>`. Git checks out a midpoint; you run your test and answer `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`. When the range collapses to one commit, Git announces it as the first bad commit. `git bisect reset` returns you to your original branch.

`git bisect run <script>` fully automates the search: the script must exit 0 for good and non-zero for bad (exit 125 means 'skip this commit — cannot test'). This turns an afternoon of manual checkouts into one command, and it is the professional way to bisect — deterministic, repeatable, and scriptable in CI.

Bisect needs a reliable, fast test and a linear-ish history to be practical. Flaky tests poison the search (a false 'good' sends the search down the wrong half), and untestable commits should be skipped with `git bisect skip` rather than guessed at. Always bisect on a clean tree — stash or commit your work first.

example.code:
$ git bisect start
$ git bisect bad HEAD
$ git bisect good v2.4.0
Bisecting: 27 revisions left to test after this (roughly 5 steps)
$ ./run_smoke_test.sh && git bisect good || git bisect bad
... (repeat at each checkout) ...
9f8e7d6a1b2 is the first bad commit
commit 9f8e7d6a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d
Author: dev@example.com
    Refactor connection pool sizing
$ git bisect reset
example.walkthrough: We mark HEAD as bad and the v2.4.0 tag as good; Git reports 27 revisions remain — about 5 test rounds. At each midpoint checkout we run the smoke test and report the verdict, halving the range each time. Git finally identifies the connection-pool refactor as the first bad commit, and `git bisect reset` restores the original branch. The whole hunt took 5 test runs instead of 27.

pitfalls: Bisecting with a flaky test: one wrong verdict sends the binary search down the wrong half and it confidently blames an innocent commit. Stabilize or quarantine the test first.
Forgetting `git bisect reset`: you end up working on a detached HEAD at some midpoint commit, and later commits seem to 'vanish' until you reset.
Bisecting a dirty tree: uncommitted changes can make the checked-out midpoint untestable or, worse, get carried into your verdicts. Stash first.
lessons.try_it: In a scratch repo with ~16 commits where one breaks a test script, use `git bisect run ./test.sh` to find the culprit automatically, then `git bisect reset`.

lessons.title: Submodules vs Subtrees: Composing Repos
concepts: A submodule nests one Git repository inside another as a pinned commit: the superproject stores a `.gitmodules` file and a gitlink (a special index entry recording the submodule's exact SHA). Cloners must run `git clone --recurse-submodules` or `git submodule update --init`, and the submodule stays at its pinned SHA until someone explicitly updates it — reproducible, but every consumer must learn submodule commands.

A subtree merges another repository's history directly into a subdirectory of your own repo (`git subtree add --prefix=lib/foo <url> <branch>`). The result is a single repository with unified history — no special clone flags, no detached-HEAD submodule states. The cost is a larger, noisier history and more complex commands when splitting changes back upstream.

Rule of thumb: use submodules when the nested project has its own release cycle, its own team, and consumers who should opt into updates deliberately (vendored SDKs, shared libraries). Use subtrees when you want the code to feel like part of your repo and your team owns both sides, or when submodule UX friction keeps biting new hires.

The classic submodule traps: forgetting `--recurse-submodules` on clone (empty directories), committing in the submodule but forgetting to commit the updated gitlink in the superproject (CI builds the old SHA), and detached-HEAD confusion when the submodule checks out a SHA rather than a branch. Subtree's trap is the reverse: `git subtree split`/`push` syntax is arcane and easy to get wrong under pressure.

example.code:
$ git submodule add https://github.com/org/shared-libs.git lib/shared
Cloning into 'lib/shared'...
$ git status
new file:   .gitmodules
new file:   lib/shared        # gitlink: pinned SHA, not files
$ cat .gitmodules
[submodule "lib/shared"]
	path = lib/shared
	url = https://github.com/org/shared-libs.git

# consumers must init:
$ git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/org/app.git
example.walkthrough: Adding the submodule clones the nested repo and records two things: the `.gitmodules` file (path and URL) and a gitlink in the index pinning the exact SHA. Note that `git status` shows `lib/shared` as a single new entry, not thousands of files — the superproject tracks only the pointer. Consumers who clone without `--recurse-submodules` get an empty `lib/shared` directory, the most common submodule support ticket.

pitfalls: Committing inside the submodule but not the superproject: CI checks out the old pinned SHA, so your fix silently never ships — always commit the updated gitlink too.
Treating the submodule checkout as a branch: it is a detached HEAD at the pinned SHA; committing there then updating the remote creates confusion about where work lives.
Choosing submodules for tightly-coupled code owned by one team: the ceremony (init, update, double commits) taxes every workflow for no isolation benefit — subtree or a monorepo fits better.
lessons.try_it: Create two scratch repos; add one as a submodule of the other, commit the gitlink, then clone the superproject with and without `--recurse-submodules` and compare.

lessons.title: Workflow Anatomy: Triggers, Jobs, Steps
concepts: A workflow is a YAML file in `.github/workflows/` that GitHub runs in response to events. The `on:` block declares triggers — `push`, `pull_request`, `schedule` (cron), `workflow_dispatch` (manual button), and more. One file can listen to many events, and filters like `branches:` or `paths:` narrow when it fires.

Inside a workflow, `jobs:` are the units of parallel execution: each job runs on a fresh virtual machine (or container) specified by `runs-on`, and jobs run in parallel unless linked with `needs:`. Within a job, `steps:` run sequentially — each step is either a shell `run:` command or a `uses:` reference to an Action (a reusable unit someone else packaged).

Actions are the ecosystem's leverage: `actions/checkout@v4` clones your repo, `actions/setup-node@v4` installs Node, and marketplace actions cover deploys, linting, and releases. Pinning to a major version tag (`@v4`) balances stability with security updates; pinning to a full SHA is the maximum-security option for sensitive pipelines.

The event payload drives logic: `github.event.pull_request.number`, `github.ref_name`, and `github.sha` let steps adapt — e.g., deploying only when the ref is a tag. `if:` conditions on jobs and steps (like `if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'`) keep one workflow file serving CI and CD differently per trigger.

example.code:
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
example.walkthrough: This minimal CI workflow triggers on pushes to main and on every pull request. The single `test` job gets a fresh Ubuntu runner, checks out the code, installs Node 20 with npm caching enabled, then runs a clean install (`npm ci`, which respects the lockfile) followed by the test suite. Any non-zero exit fails the step, the job, and marks the PR's checks red.

pitfalls: Triggering on every push with no path filters: docs-only commits burn runner minutes and queue time — add `paths:` filters for expensive jobs.
Unpinned or floating action refs (`@main`, `@master`): a compromised or breaking upstream change instantly hits your pipeline — pin to major versions at minimum.
Putting secrets in `run:` echo statements or step outputs: they can land in logs — use the `secrets` context and GitHub's automatic masking, never print them.
lessons.try_it: Create a repo (or scratch dir), add this workflow file, push a branch, open a PR, and watch the Actions tab run the pipeline. Then add a `paths:` filter and observe a docs-only push skipping the job.

lessons.title: Runners & the Build Matrix
concepts: `runs-on` selects the execution environment: GitHub-hosted runners (`ubuntu-latest`, `windows-latest`, `macos-latest`) are managed VMs billed by the minute, while self-hosted runners are machines you register for custom hardware, private network access, or cost control. Labels route jobs: `runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, gpu]` picks a matching runner.

The matrix strategy fans one job definition out across combinations: `strategy: { matrix: { os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest], node: [18, 20] } }` produces four jobs. Each combination appears as `matrix.os` / `matrix.node` variables. `fail-fast: false` lets all combinations finish even if one fails, so you see the full compatibility picture.

Self-hosted runners trade control for responsibility: you patch the OS, isolate jobs (ephemeral VMs or containers per job are best practice), and secure the runner — a compromised workflow on a persistent self-hosted runner can poison subsequent jobs or reach your network. Never run untrusted PR workflows on self-hosted runners with broad access.

Larger runners and runner groups (organization-level) let platform teams offer standardized environments — e.g., a `prod-deploy` group limited to main-branch workflows. Concurrency controls (`concurrency: { group: ..., cancel-in-progress: true }`) auto-cancel stale PR runs when new commits land, saving minutes and giving faster feedback.

example.code:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
        node: [18, 20]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
      - run: npm ci && npm test
example.walkthrough: The matrix declares two OSes and two Node versions, producing four parallel jobs (ubuntu/18, ubuntu/20, windows/18, windows/20). `fail-fast: false` ensures a Windows-only failure doesn't hide an Ubuntu problem. Each job interpolates its combination via `${{ matrix.os }}` and `${{ matrix.node }}`, so one job definition tests the full compatibility surface.

pitfalls: Exploding matrix combinations: 4 OSes x 5 versions x 3 archs = 60 jobs per push — use `include`/`exclude` to trim to supported combos and `max-parallel` to cap concurrency.
Running PRs from forks on privileged self-hosted runners: fork PRs can exfiltrate secrets or pivot into your network — restrict them to GitHub-hosted runners.
Forgetting `cancel-in-progress`: rapid pushers stack up full matrix runs per commit, multiplying minutes — add a concurrency group keyed by ref.
lessons.try_it: Add a 2x2 matrix to a scratch workflow and watch four jobs fan out in the Actions UI. Then add `concurrency` with `cancel-in-progress: true`, push twice quickly, and confirm the first run cancels.

lessons.title: Caching & Artifacts: Speeding Up Pipelines
concepts: Dependencies dominate CI time: `actions/cache` (or built-in caching in setup actions, e.g. `setup-node`'s `cache: npm`) stores directories like `~/.npm` keyed by a hash of the lockfile. A cache hit skips the download-and-install phase; the key must include the lockfile hash so dependency changes invalidate correctly, with `restore-keys` offering prefix fallbacks.

Artifacts (`actions/upload-artifact` / `download-artifact`) pass files between jobs — build once in job A, test the built output in jobs B and C — and preserve outputs (binaries, test reports, coverage) after the run. They are not a cache: artifacts are immutable per run and retained per the repo's retention policy, while caches are mutable and shared across runs.

Cache poisoning is a real threat model: if a PR workflow writes to the cache scope that main-branch builds read, a malicious PR can plant a compromised dependency. Mitigate with `actions/cache` scope isolation (PRs get their own cache namespace by default in newer versions) and by never letting untrusted code write to caches consumed by privileged jobs.

Measure before optimizing: the Actions UI shows per-step timing — attack the tallest bar first. Common wins: caching dependency installs, splitting lint/typecheck/test into parallel jobs, and `npm ci` over `npm install`. A 20-minute pipeline usually has one 14-minute step hiding in it.

example.code:
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with:
    node-version: 20
    cache: npm
- run: npm ci
# --- pass the build to the test job ---
- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: dist
    path: dist/
# --- in the downstream job ---
- uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: dist
    path: dist/
example.walkthrough: The setup-node step enables npm caching keyed on the lockfile automatically — dependency changes invalidate the cache, identical lockfiles hit it. Later, the build job uploads the `dist/` output as a named artifact; a downstream test job downloads it instead of rebuilding. Build once, test many: less duplicated work and guaranteed consistency between jobs.

pitfalls: Caching `node_modules` directly instead of the package-manager cache: restores are slower and more brittle — cache the download cache (`~/.npm`), let `npm ci` do the fast local install.
Using artifacts as a cross-run cache: artifacts are per-run and immutable — for sharing across runs you want `actions/cache`, not artifacts.
Letting fork PRs write to shared caches: a malicious dependency can be planted for privileged builds to consume — isolate cache scopes for untrusted runs.
lessons.try_it: Time a scratch workflow's install step, enable caching, and compare the before/after step durations in the Actions UI. Then upload a file as an artifact in one job and download it in another.

lessons.title: Secrets & OIDC: Authenticating Without Long-Lived Keys
concepts: GitHub secrets (`Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions`) inject sensitive values as environment variables via the `secrets` context: `${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }}`. GitHub automatically masks secret values in logs, and secrets are not passed to workflows triggered by fork PRs — a deliberate protection against exfiltration.

Long-lived static credentials are the anti-pattern: an AWS access key stored as a secret works until it leaks, and then it works for the attacker too. OpenID Connect (OIDC) replaces stored keys with short-lived tokens: GitHub mints a JWT asserting the workflow's identity (`repo`, `ref`, environment), and the cloud provider's IAM trusts GitHub's OIDC issuer and exchanges the JWT for temporary credentials.

The OIDC setup has two halves: in AWS IAM, create an identity provider for `token.actions.githubusercontent.com` with a trust policy conditioning on `sub` (e.g. `repo:org/app:ref:refs/heads/main`); in the workflow, request the token with `permissions: { id-token: write }` and use `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` with `role-to-assume`. No secret is stored anywhere — credentials live for the job's duration.

Environments add governance: define a `production` environment with required reviewers and a wait timer, then gate the deploy job with `environment: production`. Combined with OIDC scoped to `environment:production`, you get deployments that require human approval and mint credentials only for that approved run.

example.code:
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/github-deploy
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: ./deploy.sh   # AWS creds are temporary env vars
example.walkthrough: The workflow requests an OIDC token (`id-token: write`) and nothing else sensitive. `configure-aws-credentials` exchanges GitHub's JWT for short-lived AWS credentials scoped to the deploy role — no static key exists to leak. The `environment: production` gate means this job waits for a required reviewer's approval before the credentials are even minted.

pitfalls: Storing cloud keys as long-lived secrets and never rotating them: every leak is permanent until someone notices — prefer OIDC so there is nothing to rotate.
Over-broad OIDC trust policies (`sub: repo:org/*`): any workflow in any repo of the org can assume the role — condition on the exact repo and ref.
