Scripted-pipeline Groovy sprawl: 500 lines of imperative script nobody can read — prefer declarative structure, isolate custom logic in shared libraries.
lessons.try_it: Convert a freestyle-job mental model (or scratch script) into a declarative Jenkinsfile with three stages, a `when`-gated deploy, and a `post` block. Validate syntax with the Jenkins linter if available.

lessons.title: Shared Libraries: DRY for Pipelines
concepts: When ten Jenkinsfiles copy the same 40-line 'build, test, scan, publish' sequence, the fix is a Jenkins shared library: a separate repo with `vars/` (global functions like `vars/standardBuild.groovy`) and `src/` (classes), loaded via `@Library('my-lib') _`. Update the library once; every pipeline inherits it — the Jenkins equivalent of reusable workflows.

Library design mirrors software design: `vars/deployToEnv.groovy` encapsulates one well-named operation with parameters (`deployToEnv(environment: 'staging', version: env.BUILD_NUMBER)`), versioned by Git tag or branch. Consumers pin versions (`@Library('my-lib@1.x')`) so library changes roll out deliberately, not as surprise breakage across 50 pipelines.

Testing shared libraries is non-optional: the JenkinsPipelineUnit framework lets you unit-test `vars/` steps without a running Jenkins. An untested shared library is a single point of failure for every pipeline that consumes it — one bad merge becomes an org-wide build outage.

The governance balance: libraries standardize the paved road (security scanning, artifact publishing) while pipelines keep escape hatches (custom stages where needed). A library that forbids all customization gets forked around; one that's purely optional gets ignored. Version, document, and announce — treat it as a product.

example.walkthrough: The shared library defines `standardBuild` once — build, test with published results, and image scan. Each consumer Jenkinsfile shrinks to a `@Library` annotation plus a parameterized call pinned to `@1.x`. When the platform team adds SBOM generation to the standard, they edit the library; all fifty consumers get it without touching their Jenkinsfiles.

pitfalls: Untested shared library changes: one bad merge breaks every consumer pipeline simultaneously — unit-test vars/ steps with JenkinsPipelineUnit and canary the rollout.
Unpinned `@Library('my-lib')` (floating master): consumers absorb breaking changes without warning — version the library and pin consumers.
Library as a dumping ground: 200 unrelated helpers with no docs — keep it small, named, documented; it's a product, not a junk drawer.
lessons.try_it: Extract a repeated 3-stage sequence from a scratch Jenkinsfile into a `vars/` shared-library step, then consume it from two pipelines pinned to a version.

lessons.title: Credentials Binding in Jenkins
concepts: Jenkins credentials (`Manage Jenkins > Credentials`) store secrets centrally — username/password, secret text, SSH keys, certificates — in an encrypted store, scoped to system, folder, or job level. Pipelines never contain secret values; they reference credential IDs, and Jenkins injects the values as masked environment variables at runtime.

The binding mechanism: `withCredentials([string(credentialsId: 'api-token', variable: 'API_TOKEN')]) { sh './deploy.sh' }` exposes the secret only inside the block, and Jenkins masks the value in console output. `usernamePassword` bindings split into `USERNAME`/`PASSWORD` variables; `sshUserPrivateKey` writes a temporary key file. The secret value never appears in the Jenkinsfile, the job config, or (normally) the logs.

Scope credentials narrowly: a deploy token needed by one folder's jobs lives in that folder's store, not the global store. And rotate through the store — updating the credential object updates every consumer at once, which is the payoff for centralization versus secrets scattered across ten Jenkinsfiles.

The sharp edges: `env` leakage (a step that dumps all environment variables prints secrets — masking catches known values but encoded exfiltration can slip through), overly broad credential access (any job in scope can read them — including PR builds from forks, which must be sandboxed), and credentials in pipeline replay (the 'replay with edited script' feature can expose secrets to anyone with replay permission — restrict it).

example.walkthrough: The `withCredentials` block binds two credentials by ID — a secret text and a username/password pair — into environment variables visible only inside the block. The deploy script consumes them as ordinary env vars while Jenkins masks their values in the console log. The Jenkinsfile contains IDs, never values; rotation means updating the credential object once.

pitfalls: Hardcoding secrets in the Jenkinsfile: it's in git history forever and visible to every repo reader — always bind by credential ID.
Global-scoped credentials for everything: any job (including untrusted PR builds) can read them — scope to the narrowest folder/job that needs them.
Granting Replay permission broadly: edited-script replay can print secrets — restrict replay to trusted admins.
lessons.try_it: Store a dummy secret text credential in a scratch Jenkins (or simulate the pattern), bind it in a pipeline, echo it, and confirm Jenkins masks the value in the output.

lessons.title: Semantic Release Automation
concepts: Semantic release automates versioning from commit messages: commits following Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `BREAKING CHANGE:`) determine the next version — `fix:` bumps patch, `feat:` bumps minor, breaking changes bump major. The release pipeline computes the version, generates the changelog from commit messages, tags, and publishes — no human decides the version number.

The discipline that makes it work is commit hygiene: every commit message becomes user-facing changelog content, so `fix: resolve race in token refresh` is good and `fix stuff` is a changelog embarrassment. Commitlint in the PR pipeline enforces the format mechanically — the version math only works on well-formed input.

The pipeline shape: on merge to main, run tests, then the semantic-release step analyzes commits since the last tag, determines the bump, updates the changelog, creates the GitHub release, publishes the package, and pushes the tag. Failed tests mean no release — the version number is a certificate that the gates passed.

When not to use it: libraries with marketing-driven versions ('2.0' for the big launch), or teams that can't sustain commit discipline. The escape hatch is manual release config for exceptional versions — but every manual version is a process smell to investigate, not a routine.

example.code:
# .releaserc.json
{
  "branches": ["main"],
  "plugins": [
    "@semantic-release/commit-analyzer",
    "@semantic-release/release-notes-generator",
    "@semantic-release/changelog",
    "@semantic-release/git",
    "@semantic-release/github"
  ]
}
# feat: add SSO -> minor bump, changelog entry, GitHub release, tag v1.5.0
example.walkthrough: The semantic-release config declares the plugins that implement the pipeline: analyze commits, generate notes, update the changelog file, commit it back, and create the GitHub release. A `feat:` commit merged to main produces a minor bump, a changelog entry, and a published release with zero human version decisions — the commit message was the release specification.

pitfalls: Adopting semantic release with undisciplined commits: `fix stuff` becomes the public changelog — enforce Conventional Commits with commitlint first.
Manual version bumps alongside automation: the two systems fight and tags lie — commit to automation or don't, no hybrids.
Releasing from feature branches: the version math assumes a linear main history — release from main only, branch builds get prerelease tags.
lessons.try_it: In a scratch repo, install commitlint, make a `feat:` and a `fix:` commit, and run semantic-release in dry-run mode to see the version it would compute.

lessons.title: Feature Flags: Decoupling Deploy from Release
concepts: Feature flags decouple deployment (code reaching production) from release (users seeing the feature): the code ships dark behind a flag (`if (flags.newCheckout) { ... }`), and the flag flips at release time — instantly, without a deploy. Rollback becomes a flag flip, not a redeploy.

The rollout patterns: boolean kill-switches (instant off when the feature misbehaves), percentage rollouts (1% → 10% → 100% with metric watching), targeted cohorts (internal users first, then beta), and entitlement flags (feature available per plan tier). A flagging platform (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or a homegrown service) manages targeting and audit trails.

Flags are technical debt with a purpose — and they must be retired. Every flag adds a code path that must be tested; a codebase with 200 stale flags is unmaintainable. The discipline: each flag gets an owner and an expiry (remove the flag and the dead path within N weeks of full rollout), tracked like any other debt.

Flag hygiene in incidents: the first question for any feature-related outage is 'can we flag it off?' If the answer requires a deploy, the flag failed its primary job. Kill-switches for risky features should be tested (flip it in staging) before they're needed at 2 AM.

example.walkthrough: The new checkout flow ships to production in the same deploy as always — but only executes for users in the flag's 10% cohort. The release is a flag configuration change, not a code deploy. When the incident hits, disabling the flag returns all traffic to the proven legacy flow in seconds; the code fix can then proceed without time pressure.

pitfalls: Flags without retirement: 200 stale flags, each doubling test paths — every flag needs an owner and a removal date.
Flagging without targeting: a global boolean is just a config toggle — use cohorts and percentages for safe rollouts.
Kill-switch never tested: discovering at 2 AM that the flag doesn't actually disable the code path — exercise kill-switches in staging regularly.
lessons.try_it: Add a simple flag check to a scratch app (env-var-backed), deploy it 'dark,' then 'release' by flipping the variable — no redeploy. Then practice the kill-switch: break the feature and recover via the flag.

lessons.title: Hotfix Workflow: From Main to Prod
concepts: Hotfixes are production bug fixes that can't wait for the release train: the workflow must be fast, safe, and auditable. The standard shape: branch from the production tag (`git checkout -b hotfix/x v1.4.2`), fix with minimal change, run the targeted test suite, get expedited review, tag (`v1.4.3`), deploy via the normal pipeline — then forward-merge the fix into main so the release train carries it too.

Minimal change is the discipline: a hotfix is not the time for the refactor you've been wanting. Small diff, targeted tests, one concern. Every extra line is risk without a full QA cycle behind it — the hotfix gets less verification than a normal release, so it must carry less change.

Expedited review is still review: the hotfix PR needs at least one qualified reviewer and the automated gates, even at 2 AM. 'Emergency' has been used to justify unreviewed production changes since forever; the process should make the fast path also the reviewed path (on-call reviewer rotation, not 'whoever is awake').

The forward-merge is the step teams forget: the hotfix branch merges back into main (or the fix is cherry-picked), otherwise the next release reintroduces the bug. Track hotfixes as first-class releases (version bump, changelog entry, postmortem for the bug) — they're production changes, not side quests.

example.code:
$ git checkout -b hotfix/session-timeout v1.4.2
# ... minimal fix + regression test ...
$ git commit -m 'fix: extend session timeout validation (hotfix)'
$ git tag v1.4.3 && git push origin hotfix/session-timeout v1.4.3
# PR -> expedited review -> CI gates -> merge -> pipeline deploys v1.4.3
$ git checkout main && git merge hotfix/session-timeout  # forward-merge!
example.walkthrough: The hotfix branches from the production tag — not from main, which may contain unreleased work. The minimal fix commits with a clear message, gets tagged as a patch release, and flows through the normal pipeline (review + gates, expedited). The final forward-merge into main is the critical hygiene step: without it, the next release train resurrects the bug.

pitfalls: Branching the hotfix from main: main contains unreleased features — the 'hotfix' ships them too; always branch from the production tag.
Skipping review 'because emergency': the highest-risk change gets the least scrutiny — expedite the review, don't eliminate it.
Forgetting the forward-merge: the bug returns in the next release and everyone is confused — merge the hotfix back immediately.
lessons.try_it: Simulate a hotfix in a scratch repo: tag v1.0.0, advance main with a feature, branch the hotfix from the tag, fix, tag v1.0.1, forward-merge to main, and verify main has both.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: This bootcamp is organized into domains — Git Core, Branching & Merging, CI Concepts, GitHub Actions, Secret Management, and more — each containing lessons (concept teaching with real examples) and scenarios (decision-based drills that simulate on-the-job judgment calls). Work domains in order the first time; revisit weak ones via the drill mode later.

Every lesson follows the same anatomy: concepts explain the why, the example shows real commands or configs with a walkthrough, pitfalls name the traps practitioners actually hit, and the try-it gives you a hands-on exercise. Don't just read — the try-it reps are where the knowledge becomes skill.

Scenarios are the assessment engine: each presents a realistic situation, asks for a decision, and explains the reasoning in depth. They're designed like the judgment questions in technical interviews — the 'why' teaches the mental model, not just the answer. Aim to explain the why in your own words before checking.

Labs are guided hands-on exercises with step-by-step instructions and verification checks. Do them in a scratch environment (a local VM, container, or cloud sandbox) — never practice destructive Git or pipeline operations on a real repo until the motions are automatic.

example.code:
# your study loop per domain
1. read the lesson (concepts + example)
2. do the try-it exercise hands-on
3. attempt the scenario BEFORE reading the why
4. re-read the why; restate it in your own words
5. run the lab end-to-end
6. drill weak scenarios again in 3 days
example.walkthrough: The study loop turns each domain into a repeatable routine: read, practice, test yourself on the scenario before peeking at the explanation, restate the reasoning, run the lab, and spaced-repetition the weak spots. Following this loop for every domain is the difference between 'read about Git' and 'can do Git under pressure.'

pitfalls: Skipping the try-it and labs: reading about rebase is not the same as rebasing — the hands-on reps are where judgment forms.
Reading scenario answers before attempting: the retrieval effort is the learning — attempt first, then study the why.
Doing everything in one marathon session: spaced repetition beats cramming — spread domains across days and revisit weak scenarios.
lessons.try_it: Pick one domain, run the full six-step study loop on its first lesson and scenario, and note which step taught you the most.

lessons.title: Study Strategy for Git & DevOps
concepts: Git & DevOps is a doing discipline: the exam and the interview both test what you do under realistic conditions, not what you can recite. Weight your time toward hands-on reps — rebasing, resolving conflicts, writing workflows, debugging pipelines — at roughly a 70/30 practice-to-theory ratio. If your fingers haven't done it, you don't know it.

Build a personal command reference as you go: every time a lesson teaches a command sequence (rebase todo lists, cherry-pick with -x, OIDC trust policies), write it in your own words with an example. This becomes your interview cheat sheet and your on-call runbook — the act of writing it is itself the studying.

Learn the failure modes, not just the happy paths: interviewers probe judgment with 'what goes wrong when...' questions. For every tool, know its sharp edges (force-push without lease, :latest tags, stale submodule pins, unscoped OIDC trust) — the pitfalls sections of each lesson are interview gold.

Simulate the real thing weekly: pick a scenario you got wrong, rebuild the situation in a scratch repo, and practice the recovery until it's boring. Incident-response calm comes from reps, not from reading — the engineer who has rescued a detached HEAD five times doesn't panic the sixth.

example.code:
# weekly practice cadence
Mon/Wed/Fri: 1 new domain (lesson + try-it + scenarios)
Tue/Thu:     labs for the week's domains
Sat:         45-min timed scenario drill (mixed domains)
Sun:         rest + review personal command reference
# rule: no new domain until last week's scenarios score 80%+
example.walkthrough: The weekly cadence balances new material with reinforcement: new domains on alternate days, labs consolidating them, a timed mixed drill on Saturday simulating assessment pressure, and a gate — 80%+ on last week's scenarios before advancing. The command reference review on Sunday keeps the sharp edges fresh.

pitfalls: Theory-only studying: you can explain rebase but can't perform one — the interview's live exercise exposes this instantly.
Advancing with weak fundamentals: shaky Git core makes every advanced topic harder — honor the 80% gate before moving on.
Practicing only happy paths: the job is 90% debugging — deliberately practice recoveries (bad resets, failed workflows, leaked secrets).
lessons.try_it: Set up your scratch environment this week (local repos, a free CI-capable repo, a container runtime) and complete the first domain's try-it exercises in it.

lessons.title: Course Map: From Git Core to DevOps Culture
concepts: The course is sequenced deliberately. Foundations: Git Core, Branching & Merging, Remotes & Collaboration — the version-control fluency every DevOps role assumes. You must be able to stage, branch, merge, rebase, and collaborate before anything else makes sense.

Automation layer: CI Concepts, Jenkins Basics, GitHub Actions, Container Workflows — how code becomes tested artifacts automatically. This is where Git knowledge compounds: pipelines are Git-driven automation, and every scenario here assumes you can read a repo's history.

Delivery layer: Release Flow, Advanced Git Surgery, Secret Management — shipping safely at scale. Versioning, hotfixes, feature flags, and secret lifecycles are the difference between 'can deploy' and 'can be trusted with production.'

Human layer: DevOps Culture & Practices — CALMS, DORA, postmortems, platform thinking. Senior interviews weight this heavily: tools get you the interview, judgment about systems and people gets you the offer. The capstone then integrates all four layers into one shipped pipeline.

example.code:
foundations:    git-core -> branching-merging -> remotes-collab
  automation:   ci-concepts -> jenkins | github-actions -> container-workflows
  delivery:     release-flow -> advanced-git -> secret-management
  human:        devops-culture (threads through all layers)
  capstone:     ship a full pipeline integrating all four
example.walkthrough: The map shows the dependency chain: foundations enable automation (pipelines are Git-driven), automation enables delivery (you can't release safely what you can't build reliably), and culture threads through everything. The arrows are prerequisites — struggling with GitHub Actions usually means a Git Core gap, not an Actions gap. The capstone at the end proves the integration.

pitfalls: Skipping foundations to 'get to the interesting stuff': every advanced topic assumes Git fluency — the map's arrows are real prerequisites.
Treating culture as optional: senior loops weight CALMS/DORA/postmortem judgment heavily — it's a hiring signal, not filler.
Doing the capstone first: it's an integration exercise — without the layers, it's just frustrating; with them, it's the proof.
lessons.try_it: Draw the course map from memory, then check it against this lesson. For any domain you can't place, read its first lesson before continuing.

lessons.title: Assessment & Interview Strategy
concepts: Technical assessments for Git & DevOps roles come in three flavors: scenario judgment ('a teammate force-pushed — what do you do?'), live exercises ('rebase these commits into a clean history'), and system design ('design the CI/CD for this org'). This bootcamp's scenarios train the first, try-its and labs train the second, and the culture domain trains the third.

For scenario questions, use the structure: identify the constraint (what must not break), name the mechanism (which Git/CI feature applies), choose the minimal safe action, and state the verification (how you'd confirm). Interviewers score the reasoning chain, not just the answer — narrate your thinking the way the scenario 'why' sections do.

For live exercises, narrate as you type: 'I'm checking which branch I'm on before rebasing, because rebasing the wrong branch is the classic mistake.' This turns the exercise into evidence of judgment, not just typing. And always verify after destructive operations — `git status`, `git log`, pipeline run — before declaring done.

For 'tell me about a time' questions, mine your lab and capstone work: 'When I built the capstone pipeline, the cache kept serving stale dependencies — I keyed it on the lockfile hash and the install step dropped from four minutes to twenty seconds.' Real reps become real stories; stories beat recitations.

example.code:
# scenario answer structure (say this out loud)
1. constraint: what must not break? (prod, history, secrets)
2. mechanism: which feature applies? (rebase, OIDC, canary...)
3. action: minimal safe step
4. verify: how do I confirm? (log, status, metrics)
# live exercise narration
$ git status          # 'checking my branch before the rebase'
$ git rebase -i main  # 'rewriting only my feature commits'
example.walkthrough: The four-step structure (constraint → mechanism → action → verify) is a speaking framework for scenario questions — it demonstrates judgment, not just knowledge. The live-exercise example shows narration: each command is paired with the reasoning a senior engineer would voice. Practicing this narration during labs makes it automatic in interviews.

pitfalls: Answering scenarios with just the letter: interviewers score reasoning — narrate constraint, mechanism, action, verification.
Silent live exercises: the interviewer can't distinguish skill from luck — narrate every non-obvious decision as you type.
Generic 'tell me about a time' answers: mine your labs and capstone for specific, quantified stories instead.
lessons.try_it: Take one scenario you already completed and answer it out loud using the four-step structure. Record yourself and check: did you state the constraint first?

lessons.title: Capstone Architecture: The System You'll Build
concepts: The capstone is a complete delivery system for a sample web service: a Git repository with protected main, feature-branch workflow, and CODEOWNERS; a GitHub Actions pipeline (lint → test → build → scan → push); multi-stage Docker images tagged immutably and promoted through environments; secrets via OIDC with no static credentials; and releases via semantic versioning with feature flags for rollout.

Architecture decisions to make upfront: monorepo vs polyrepo for the sample (polyrepo keeps it focused), GitHub-hosted vs self-hosted runners (hosted — no infra to maintain), registry choice (GitHub Container Registry keeps auth simple), and deployment target (a small cloud VM or PaaS — the point is the pipeline, not the hosting exoticism).

The branching model: short-lived feature branches, PRs with required checks and code-owner review, squash-merge to main for linear history, tags for releases. Document the model in CONTRIBUTING.md — the capstone is evaluated partly on whether another engineer could follow your process.

Observability of the pipeline itself: build-time dashboards (DORA metrics for your one repo — lead time, failure rate), pipeline notifications, and a runbook for the pipeline's own failures. A pipeline nobody monitors is a pipeline that fails silently the week before the demo.

example.code:
# capstone repo layout
.github/workflows/ci.yml        # lint, test, build, scan
.github/workflows/release.yml  # tag -> version, changelog, publish
.github/CODEOWNERS
Dockerfile                      # multi-stage
compose.yaml                    # local dev stack
CONTRIBUTING.md                 # branching model + release process
infra/                          # deploy configs
# environments: dev (auto) -> staging (auto) -> prod (manual approval)
example.walkthrough: The repo layout is the architecture made concrete: two workflows separating CI from release, CODEOWNERS for review routing, a multi-stage Dockerfile, Compose for local parity, and documented process. The environment progression (auto dev/staging, gated prod) demonstrates deployment-strategy thinking, and the DORA tracking shows you measure the system you built.

pitfalls: Building the pipeline before the branching model: the pipeline encodes the process — decide the process first, then automate it.
Skipping the docs (CONTRIBUTING.md, runbooks): an undocumented pipeline is a personal script, not engineering — document as you build.
Gold-plating the hosting: the capstone proves delivery competence, not infrastructure exoticism — keep the target boring and the pipeline excellent.
lessons.try_it: Create the capstone repo skeleton: the directory layout above, an empty ci.yml with stage comments, and a one-page ARCHITECTURE.md stating your decisions and why.

lessons.title: Capstone Build Guide: From Empty Repo to Green Pipeline
concepts: Phase 1 — Repository: initialize with main protection (require PRs, required checks, code-owner review), CODEOWNERS, CONTRIBUTING.md with the branching model, and commitlint. Verify: try pushing to main directly and confirm it's rejected.

Phase 2 — CI: write ci.yml (checkout, setup, lint, unit tests, build). Add caching keyed on the lockfile, matrix over two Node versions, and path filters. Break it on purpose (failing test) and confirm the PR goes red with a useful message — a pipeline you've never seen fail is a pipeline you don't trust.

Phase 3 — Containers & security: multi-stage Dockerfile, image build + Trivy scan in CI (fail on critical), push to GHCR with immutable tags (version + SHA). Add gitleaks pre-commit and push protection. Verify: the scan gate actually blocks a deliberately vulnerable base image.

Phase 4 — Delivery: release workflow on tags (semantic-release), OIDC-based deploy credentials, environment protection rules (manual approval for prod), feature flag for the demo feature, canary or blue-green deploy to your target. Then run the DORA numbers on your own repo for the final report.

example.code:
# phase 2 verification checklist
[ ] direct push to main rejected
[ ] PR with failing test goes red with clear message
[ ] docs-only push skips heavy jobs (path filter)
[ ] cache hit: install step < 30s on unchanged deps
[ ] matrix: 2 Node versions x 1 OS all green
[ ] failing Trivy scan blocks the image push
example.walkthrough: The build guide is phased so each layer is verified before the next is built: repo protections first (prove the guardrails work by attacking them), then CI (prove it fails usefully), then containers and security gates (prove they block), then delivery. The checklists turn 'I think it works' into demonstrated behavior — which is also exactly what you'll demo.

pitfalls: Building all four phases then testing: when it breaks you won't know which layer — verify each phase's checklist before proceeding.
Never testing the failure paths: approving a pipeline that's never gone red is faith-based engineering — break it deliberately, every gate.
Skipping the DORA self-measurement: the final report's numbers (your lead time, your failure rate) are the proof the system works.
lessons.try_it: Complete Phase 1 this week: protected main, CODEOWNERS, CONTRIBUTING.md. Attack your own protections (direct push, unreviewed PR) and confirm they're rejected.

lessons.title: Capstone Demo & Portfolio Packaging
concepts: The demo tells the story in 10 minutes: start from a feature branch, open the PR (show required checks and code-owner review firing), merge, watch the pipeline (test, scan, build, push with immutable tags), cut a release (changelog auto-generated), flip the feature flag for 10% of traffic, and show the DORA dashboard of your own repo. Live, narrated, no slides-only handwaving.

Prepare for the failure demo too: show the pipeline catching a deliberately introduced vulnerability (Trivy gate goes red), and the kill-switch flag disabling a broken feature in seconds. Interviewers remember the engineer who demos the safety systems, not just the happy path — it proves production judgment.

Portfolio packaging: the repo README is the landing page (architecture diagram, DORA numbers, demo video link), ARCHITECTURE.md holds decisions, and a 2-minute demo video (screen recording with narration) lives on your portfolio. Pin the repo on your GitHub profile. Quantify everything: pipeline runtime, image size reduction, vulnerability counts before/after.

The writeup: a one-page case study — problem, architecture, key decisions (with alternatives considered), measured results, what you'd do differently. This is the artifact that survives beyond the demo and the one hiring managers actually read. Link it from your resume's projects section.

example.code:
# demo script (10 min)
0:00 repo tour: protections, CODEOWNERS, workflows
2:00 open PR -> checks fire, code-owner requested
4:00 merge -> pipeline: test, scan, build, push (immutable tag)
6:00 cut release -> changelog generated, tag pushed
7:30 flag flip: feature to 10%, metrics watched
8:30 failure demo: vuln introduced -> gate goes red
9:30 kill-switch: flag off, traffic safe in seconds
example.walkthrough: The demo script is timed to the minute: it moves from process (protections, reviews) through automation (pipeline, releases) to judgment (flag rollouts, failure handling). The failure demo at 8:30 is deliberate — it demonstrates the safety systems working, which is the strongest possible evidence of production readiness. The packaging turns the live demo into durable portfolio artifacts.

pitfalls: Slides-only demo: 'here's what it would do' proves nothing — run it live, including the failure paths.
Demoing only the happy path: anyone can show green builds — the red-gate and kill-switch demos are what signal senior judgment.
No quantified results: 'I built a pipeline' vs 'pipeline runs in 6 min, images 92% smaller, zero critical CVEs' — numbers make it real.
lessons.try_it: Record a 2-minute narrated screen capture of your Phase 2 pipeline running (or a dry run of the demo script's first half). Watch it back: is every step legible to a stranger?

Restore the branch with `git reset --hard <entry>` (e.g. HEAD@{1}) — verify with `git log` that all 3 commits are back.
As a bonus, create a named branch at the rescued commit instead of resetting.

checks.hint: Run `git log --oneline` — all three original commits are reachable again with their original messages.
Run `git reflog` — the recovery reset is recorded as the newest entry.

labs.success_message: You recovered 'lost' work from the reflog — resets move pointers, they don't delete commits.

labs.title: Bisect the regression
labs.objective: Find a breaking commit in a 16-commit history using automated bisect.
steps: In a scratch repo, create 16 commits where commit #11 breaks a `test.sh` script (exit 1) while earlier ones pass (exit 0).
Run `git bisect start`, mark HEAD bad and the first commit good, then `git bisect run ./test.sh`.
Record the commit Git identifies as the first bad one and confirm it's #11.
Run `git bisect reset` and verify you're back on your original branch.

checks.hint: Git's output names the first bad commit — its message matches your planted breaking change.
Run `git status` after reset — you're on the original branch, not a detached HEAD.

labs.success_message: You found one bad commit in 16 with ~4 test runs — logarithmic debugging in action.

labs.title: GitHub Actions CI from scratch
labs.objective: Build a working CI workflow with matrix builds, caching, and path filters.
steps: Create a scratch repo with a tiny Node (or Python) project and a test script.
Write `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: triggers on push/PR with `paths-ignore` for docs, a 2x2 matrix, dependency caching, and test + lint steps.
Push a code change and a docs-only change; confirm the docs push skips the heavy jobs.
Break a test on purpose, watch the PR go red, fix it, and watch it go green.

checks.hint: The Actions run list shows the docs-only push skipping (or not running) the test jobs.
The matrix run shows all combinations executed as separate jobs.

labs.success_message: You built a real CI pipeline with the cost and speed controls professionals use.

labs.title: Multi-stage Docker build
labs.objective: Cut a production image's size and vulnerability count with a multi-stage build.
steps: Write a single-stage Dockerfile for a scratch app and record `docker images` size.
Convert it to multi-stage (build stage + slim runtime stage, non-root USER), rebuild, and compare sizes.
Scan both images with Trivy or `docker scout`; record the CVE counts before/after.
Push the slim image with an immutable tag (version + git SHA).

checks.hint: Run `docker images` — the multi-stage image is dramatically smaller than the single-stage one.
The scan report shows fewer (ideally zero critical) CVEs on the slim image.

labs.success_message: You applied the two highest-leverage image practices: multi-stage builds and minimal bases.

labs.title: Compose dev environment
labs.objective: Give a scratch app a one-command reproducible dev stack with Compose.
steps: Write a `compose.yaml` with your app + a database (pinned versions), named volume for data, and env-var config.
Run `docker compose up`, verify the app reaches the database, and seed some data.
Run `docker compose down` and `up` again — confirm the seeded data survived via the named volume.
Run `docker compose config` and confirm no secrets are hardcoded in the rendered output.

checks.hint: `docker compose ps` shows both services healthy with the pinned image versions.
After down/up, the seeded data is still present (named volume worked).

labs.success_message: You built the 'works on every machine' dev environment — onboarding in one command.

labs.title: Secret scanning & response
labs.objective: Find a planted secret in git history and execute the revoke-then-purge response.
steps: In a scratch repo, commit a fake AWS-shaped key in an early commit, then 'delete' it in a later commit.
Run gitleaks over full history and confirm it finds the key despite the deletion.
Execute the response in order: revoke (simulate), purge with `git filter-repo`, force-push, re-clone.
Rescan and confirm clean; write a 5-line incident note.

checks.hint: The first gitleaks run reports the planted key with its commit SHA.
After purge + re-clone, a fresh gitleaks run reports zero findings.

labs.success_message: You ran the full leak lifecycle: detect in history, revoke first, purge second, verify last.

labs.title: OIDC trust policy design
labs.objective: Design (on paper or in a sandbox) an OIDC trust chain that eliminates a static deploy key.
steps: Pick a real or hypothetical deploy workflow that currently uses a stored cloud key.
Write the IAM trust policy conditioning on the exact repo and ref (`StringEquals` on `sub`).
Write the workflow snippet requesting `id-token: write` and assuming the role.
Document what happens on: a fork PR, a branch push, and a compromised workflow — for each, state whether credentials are mintable.

checks.hint: Your trust policy's `sub` condition names the exact repo and ref — not a wildcard.
Your analysis correctly shows fork PRs cannot mint credentials under this policy.

labs.success_message: You designed keyless deployment auth — the static secret is gone, not just better hidden.

labs.title: Blameless postmortem writing
labs.objective: Write a real postmortem for an incident (real or simulated) using the blameless structure.
steps: Pick an incident you caused or witnessed (or simulate one: break a scratch pipeline).
Build the timeline from logs, not memory; quantify impact (duration, users, errors).
Identify 3+ contributing factors — no 'human error' allowed as a root cause.
Write 2+ action items with owners and due dates; share the doc for review.

checks.hint: The timeline cites log timestamps, not recollections.
Every action item names an owner and a due date; none blame a person.

labs.success_message: You produced the artifact that turns an outage into organizational learning.

labs.title: DORA self-assessment
labs.objective: Measure the four DORA metrics for a project you work on and plan one improvement.
steps: Gather rough numbers: deploy frequency, lead time (commit→prod), change failure rate, MTTR for the last month.
Classify the performance tier per metric (elite/high/medium/low).
Identify the weakest metric and trace it to a specific capability gap (e.g., lead time ← manual approvals).
Write a one-page improvement plan: the capability investment, expected metric movement, and how you'll measure it.

checks.hint: Your writeup defines each metric precisely (e.g., lead time measured commit→prod).
The improvement plan names a concrete capability change, not just 'try harder'.

labs.success_message: You turned delivery metrics into an actionable improvement plan — the DORA loop in miniature.

labs.title: Capstone dry run: pipeline skeleton
labs.objective: Stand up the capstone repo skeleton with protections and a first green pipeline run.
steps: Create the repo with the capstone layout (workflows dir, CODEOWNERS, Dockerfile, compose.yaml, CONTRIBUTING.md).
Enable branch protection on main; verify a direct push is rejected.
Write ci.yml through the Test stage with caching; get a green run on a PR.
Record baseline numbers: pipeline runtime, image size, install-step duration — you'll improve them in the capstone.

checks.hint: A direct push to main is rejected by branch protection.
The PR shows a green CI run with the caching step hitting on the second push.

labs.success_message: Your capstone foundation stands: protected repo, working CI, and baseline metrics to beat.

simulations.title: The push that got rejected
simulations.brief: git push is rejected: the remote has commits you don't have. Nothing is lost, but the push won't go through.

steps.symptom: Push rejected — 'failed to push some refs'; the remote is ahead of your branch.
evidence:
$ git push
! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs
options: Fetch first: pull the remote's commits into your branch, resolve any conflicts, then push
Push with --force to overwrite the remote
Delete your branch and start over
steps.explain: The remote moved while you worked. Fetching first integrates their commits; force-pushing would erase someone else's work.

steps.symptom: After fetching, one file conflicts: both sides edited the same lines.
evidence:
$ git pull
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.yaml
options: Open the conflicted file, keep the correct parts of both sides, remove the markers, add and commit
steps.explain: Conflict markers are a to-do list, not a verdict. Read both sides, merge the intent, then complete the merge commit.

steps.symptom: Conflict resolved and committed. Verify the sync.
evidence:
$ git log --oneline -3
9f3a2c1 Add CI pipeline
2b1c4d5 Merge remote config fix
a1b2c3d Resolve config.yaml conflict
options: Confirm the merge commit exists and push succeeds
Confirm the conflict file is deleted
steps.explain: The merge commit joins both histories; a clean push after it proves local and remote agree.

simulations.debrief: Rejected pushes mean the remote moved first. Fetch, merge the intent (never blind-pick a side), commit the merge, push. Force-push is never the answer on shared branches.

simulations.title: Release pipeline order
simulations.brief: Restore the order of a branch-to-release flow.

steps.context: Arrange the release flow stages in execution order.
items: Create a feature branch from main
Open a pull request
Review and merge the pull request
Tag the release on main
Deploy the tagged release

simulations.debrief: Branch → PR → merge → tag → deploy. Skipping the tag is how you deploy something you can't name later.

simulations.title: Merge or rebase?
simulations.brief: Choose the integration strategy for two situations.

steps.text: Your feature branch is 3 commits behind main, and you want the latest main changes in your branch before opening the PR. The branch is only yours.

choices.label: Rebase onto main: your commits replay on the latest main — a clean, linear story
choices.feedback: Right: on a private branch, rebase keeps history linear and the PR diff minimal.

choices.label: Merge main into your branch
choices.feedback: Merging main into a private feature branch works but litters history with merge commits before review.

choices.label: Cherry-pick main's commits one by one
choices.feedback: Cherry-picking upstream changes duplicates them and confuses the later merge.

steps.text: The PR is approved. The branch has 20 tiny 'wip' commits. How does it land on main?

choices.label: Squash-merge: one clean commit on main with the PR's intent
choices.feedback: Right: main keeps one meaningful commit per PR; the 20 wips stay in the PR history for archaeology.

choices.label: Rebase-merge the 20 wips onto main
choices.feedback: 20 wip commits on main's permanent history is noise nobody can bisect through.

choices.label: Push directly to main
choices.feedback: Direct pushes to main bypass the review the PR just completed.

simulations.debrief: Private branch catching up → rebase. Approved PR landing → squash. Shared history is never rewritten; private history is yours to curate.

simulations.title: The pipeline that ran on main
simulations.brief: A Jenkins pipeline deploys from main on every push — including unreviewed pushes. The Jenkinsfile has 2 bugs in 14 lines.

issues.description: pollSCM on main rebuilds and redeploys on every push — including direct pushes that skipped review.
issues.fix: Trigger deploys from tags or a release branch, not from every main push.

issues.description: The Deploy stage runs unconditionally after Test — a green test run on an unreviewed commit still ships.
issues.fix: Gate Deploy on an approved release input or restrict it to tagged builds.

simulations.debrief: Pipelines are policy as code: triggers and stage gates decide what ships. Unconditional deploy-on-main-push is an incident waiting for a bad commit.

sections.heading: Git Core
items: Staging area — git's staging area (index) is where you assemble the next commit: git add stages specific files (or hunks with -p), git commit snapshots exactly what's staged.

Working tree — git diff = working tree vs index (unstaged changes); git diff --staged (aka --cached) = index vs HEAD (what the commit will contain); git diff main...feature = feature's unique changes vs merge-base.
Common trap — git stash push -m "wip", then pull/rebase, then git stash pop.
Common trap — git diff only shows committed changes.
Common trap — git rebase -i to rewrite any published commit freely.
Common trap — edit the old commit's files directly.

sections.heading: Branching & Merging
items: Branches — merge shared branches (main, release) to preserve true history — rebasing those rewrites commits others built on. Stale branches accumulate into a confusing forest; deleting after merge is hygiene.

Isolation — git switch -c (or checkout -b) creates a branch — a 41-byte pointer, essentially free — so the feature develops in isolation: main stays deployable, the feature's history stays reviewable, and integration happens deliberately via merge/PR.

Merge conflicts — --no-ff forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible, preserving the feature as a named unit with its integration point — git log --graph shows the branch's lifespan. The commits themselves remain reachable through the merge commit.
Common trap — rebase for private/local history (linear, reviewable); merge for shared/public history (preserves true chronology).
Common trap — merge the whole feature branch into main.
Common trap — conflicts resolve themselves on the next pull.
Common trap — pick one side with git checkout --ours for everything.

Conflicts are Git asking a human to decide — edit the file to the correct result (either side or a combination), remove the markers, git add to mark resolved, then commit to complete the merge. --ours/--theirs auto-picks are for mechanical cases (and dangerous as a default). Pull requests — then you choose: merge (preserves chronology) or rebase (linear). git pull skips the decision by merging immediately, which surprises people mid-rebase-workflow.

sections.heading: Jenkins Basics
items: Jenkinsfile — a declarative Jenkinsfile in the repo makes the pipeline code: versioned, reviewed, diffable, and reproducible per branch (multibranch pipelines build the Jenkinsfile on each branch).
Pipeline as code — post is the pipeline's finally clause — deterministic handling of every outcome.
Agents — Agents (nodes) execute builds; the controller orchestrates.
Controller isolation — running builds on the controller risks stability (a runaway build kills Jenkins) and security (builds access the controller's filesystem/credentials).
Credentials binding — the credentials store + credentials() binding injects secrets as masked env vars at runtime — the Jenkinsfile references only the credential ID.
Secrets — hardcoded secrets leak to every repo clone and build log.
Common trap — use a multibranch pipeline: Jenkins discovers branches and PRs, building each one's Jenkinsfile automatically.

Common trap — use agents (nodes): the controller orchestrates, agents execute.
Common trap — put credentials in the Jenkinsfile as plain strings.

Branching — Branching from main would drag in unreleased v2.5 work; committing to main alone leaves production unfixed.

Release branches — hotfix branches fork from the release tag (the code that's actually live), get the minimal fix, tag the patch release (v2.4.1), and merge back into both main and the release line so the fix isn't lost.

Trunk-based (short-lived branches <1 day, merge to main, feature flags for incomplete work) fits continuous delivery: main is always releasable, integration is continuous, merge hell never accumulates.
`git pull` is fetch + merge in one. What does the first half do alone — and why would you want the pause between?

git cherry-pick replays a commit's diff onto the current branch as a new commit — surgical porting without merging the whole branch. Standard for hotfixes (fix lands on main, cherry-picked to release branches).

The declarative post block runs conditionally on the build result: always (publish test reports, archive artifacts, clean workspace), failure/unstable (notify), success (promote). Without it, a failed build's evidence dies with the works…

Feature flags decouple deploy from release: the code merges continuously (no merge hell, always integrated and tested) but stays inert until the flag flips. Long branches accumulate conflicts and untested integration risk; big-bang merge…
Rebase rewrites commits. When is rewriting safe — when you're the only one who's seen them, or after they've been pushed and pulled?
Staging area: git's staging area (index) is where you assemble the next commit: git add stages specific files (or hunks with -p), git commit snapshots exactly what's staged.
Secrets: hardcoded secrets leak to every repo clone and build log.
Pipeline as code: post is the pipeline's finally clause — deterministic handling of every outcome.
